bio.en: Karri Saarinen is the co-founder and CEO of Linear, one of the most beloved issue-tracking tools for software teams, and was previously founding designer at Coinbase and principal designer at Airbnb.
bio.zh: 卡里·萨里宁（Karri Saarinen）是 Linear 的联合创始人兼 CEO，该产品是软件团队中最受青睐的任务追踪工具之一；他此前是 Coinbase 的创始设计师、Airbnb 的首席设计师。

summary.en: Karri argues that as a product category matures, design quality becomes a basic price of entry rather than a differentiator. He describes how Linear builds with extreme focus on craft, speed, and a small, high-agency team. The episode is a master class in building a fast, opinionated, design-led company.
summary.zh: 卡里认为，随着某个产品品类走向成熟，设计质量会从"差异化优势"变成"入场的基本门槛"。他讲述了 Linear 如何通过极度聚焦工艺、速度和一支小型高自驱团队来打造产品。本期堪称构建一家快速、有主张、以设计驱动的公司的大师课。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: My belief is that, like any domain or industry, the more it matters, the more the design matters. What happens is whenever there's a new paradigm, I don't know, like the mobile or the web or something the first iterations of those products existing there, they don't have to be super well designed necessarily because they are the first. (00:00:19): Then, as you build the 100,000 different email clients, any email client now has to be pretty good to be even considered an email client. It's like the bar is so high. I think today it's almost a very basic thing now. Pretty much from the very beginning, you need pretty high level design for people to even pay attention or consider you seriously.
turns.zh: 我的观点是，与任何领域或行业一样，一件事越重要，设计的重要性就越显著。每当出现新的范式时，比如移动端、网络等领域，相关产品的初代版本往往不必追求极致的设计，因为它们毕竟是开创性的。（00:00:19）但当市场上涌现出十万款不同的邮件客户端时，如今任何一款邮件客户端都必须具备相当出色的设计才能被认可。标准门槛已经极高。我认为如今这几乎已成共识。从一开始，你就需要高水准的设计，才能真正吸引用户的注意并获得他们的认真考量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe to start, set a little context, can you just explain what is Linear? What does Linear do? Then, share maybe a few stats of just the scale of Linear at this point.
turns.zh: 或许首先，我们需要做个背景介绍，你能否解释一下什么是Linear？Linear是做什么的？然后，分享一下Linear目前的规模数据。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Linear is the project and issue tracking system that software companies and technical teams love to use. We help software companies to build software. We started 2019. Today some of the top growth companies like Block, Vercel, Ramp, Retool, Mercury, and Softstack are building with Linear. We also additionally have lots of other companies, thousands of other companies using Linear. These companies can be a very early stage team like some companies just graduated from YC or a public company. (00:05:17): Just briefly, why we created Linear is that, like you said, I worked with you at Airbnb and before that I worked at Coinbase. Before that, I had my own startup. All of us founders, there's three of us, we had a similar path where we worked in multiple different companies in different stages. What we saw often is that the tools available for managing software projects weren't really cutting it. I think a lot of them felt very clunky or complex or just like they had this legacy way of thinking about software development. We just felt like we should do something about it. With Linear, we set out to build this most frictionless and streamlined system for modern software development. I'm also happy to share that we've been profitable the last two years. We also have this thing where we actually have this net negative lifetime burn rate, which means that we just have more cash in the bank today than we have raised. I think with a lot of startups usually the normal way is that you raise money and then you need to spend it to build it. I think since we were able to build a business pretty early on, we've been able to be in this position that actually we haven't spent any money on building the business.
turns.zh:
Linear是一款深受软件公司和技术团队喜爱的项目与问题追踪系统。我们致力于帮助软件公司打造优质产品。Linear成立于2019年。目前，Block、Vercel、Ramp、Retool、Mercury和Softstack等顶级成长型公司都在使用Linear。此外，我们还有数千家其他公司在使用Linear。这些公司既有初创团队，比如刚从YC毕业的公司，也有上市公司。
（00:05:17）：简要来说，我们创建Linear的原因是，正如你所说，我曾在Airbnb与你共事，在此之前我在Coinbase工作。再往前，我还创办过自己的初创公司。我们三位创始人都有相似的经历——在不同阶段、不同公司的多个岗位上工作过。当时我们发现，市面上用于管理软件项目的工具都存在严重不足。很多工具要么操作繁琐、过于复杂，要么仍固守传统的软件开发思路。我们决定必须有所改变。凭借Linear，我们致力于打造一套最顺畅、最高效的现代软件开发系统。值得一提的是，过去两年我们实现了盈利。更令人惊喜的是，我们的净负债率为负，这意味着当前银行存款远超融资额。对于多数初创公司而言，通常是先融资再投入资金建设。但由于我们较早实现了商业化，如今我们无需为业务扩张烧钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is insane. I didn't even know that. For all those reasons, a lot of founders and a lot of product leaders look up to the way Linear builds product and the way you think about product. To frame this conversation, there's three areas I want to dive into. One is just how you approach building product. Two is how you go about building the team and the business in general and then three is just how you grow Linear. To start, I want to talk about craft. (00:07:11): Clearly, one of the biggest reasons that people look up to Linear and use Linear is the quality of the user experience and the product. I know your team puts a lot of emphasis on craft and user experience. I imagine that also comes at the cost of some trade-offs like it takes probably longer to get stuff out the door. You're probably losing sales because people are waiting for a feature and you're not ready to launch it yet. You want to make it better. What have you learned about creating space for craft and building product that is really, really great?
turns.zh:
这太不可思议了。我之前完全不知道这些情况。基于以上种种原因，许多创始人和产品负责人都敬佩Linear的开发理念和产品思路。为深入探讨，我想围绕三个方面展开：一是产品开发策略；二是团队与商业模式构建；三是Linear的增长策略。首先，我想谈谈“精工精神”。
（00:07:11）：显然，人们推崇Linear、选择Linear的最重要原因之一在于其卓越的用户体验和产品品质。我知道你们团队非常注重精工和用户体验。但这或许意味着要付出代价，比如产品上线速度较慢。可能因为某些功能尚未完善，用户不得不等待而错失商机，但你们仍坚持打磨产品。请问，你们在如何为精工和产品创新创造空间方面积累了哪些深刻见解？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think it's interesting that those things you mentioned like hiring, building business, and building product and craft, I think that all of those are somewhat related to each other. What I can say about the product craft per se is it definitely starts with the people. On the hiring front, we always look for people that care about it. As a business, why we really care about it is that we see that cooperation only happens if people use the product and our product, which is supposed to help the cooperation, coordination. (00:08:14): If there's friction or the experience isn't that great or there's little paper cuts, I think it gets really annoying for people to use. We think for the business to be successful the quality and the craft is very important. There's definitely trade-offs sometimes. There can be for example timelines like we are about to launch something and then for example I or someone else goes to look at it and sees, "Oh, this doesn't feel right and we should fix it so I don't think we should launch this now." (00:08:43): Sometimes it does definitely push the timelines, but this might be days. It's not like we need to redo everything. The other way we think about it is we are actually very okay pushing things out to ourselves and for a small group of customers if they opt into that. Whenever we build a new feature one of the things is we don't want to spend tons of time upfront just designing it, then polishing it perfectly. (00:09:13): We actually believe that when you start building the thing you actually start realizing more how it should work and how it should be better. A lot of times with the teams we tell them, "Just put it there in, I don't know, the first week almost. After you have some designs in place or some design ideas, just put it into the app and ship it to production." It's only visible to us so we internally can test it out. (00:09:40): Then, I think the next stage is we look for a customer that could be interested in this feature or we just ask people to opt in to some better program. In those stages, the experience can be a little janky or it's not that polished, but we're okay with it because we are saying, "It's not finished. We just want to get your feedback early so we can make it better." Once we get to the full general release, then we pay more attention to the actual polish or the craft.
turns.zh: 我觉得很有意思的是，你提到的招聘、业务拓展以及产品打造和精细化这些事务，彼此之间存在着某种关联。就产品精细化而言，我认为它首先始于人。招聘方面，我们一直寻找那些对此充满热情的人才。就业务层面而言，我们之所以如此重视这一点，是因为我们发现，只有当人们使用我们的产品时，合作才能真正实现——而我们的产品本就旨在促进这种协作与协调。（00:08:14）：如果存在摩擦、用户体验不佳或者存在一些微小的问题，人们使用起来就会觉得很烦人。我们认为，要想让业务取得成功，产品质量和精细化至关重要。有时这确实会带来权衡。比如，当我们即将上线某项功能时，如果我或其他人去查看后发现，“哦，这个感觉不对，我们应该先修复它”，然后我们就可能推迟上线时间。（00:08:43）：有时这确实会延迟时间，但最多也就几天而已。我们并不需要全部重做。另一种考虑是，我们其实很乐意先向自己和一小群愿意参与的客户推送新功能。每当我们开发新功能时，首要任务不是花大量时间设计，而是先将其上线，然后投入生产。只有我们内部能看到这个功能。（00:09:13）：然后，我认为下一个阶段是寻找可能对该功能感兴趣的客户，或者邀请人们加入某个测试计划。在这些阶段，用户体验可能有些粗糙或不够完善，但我们不介意，因为我们会说：“它还没完成，我们只是想尽早获得反馈以便改进。”一旦全面上线，我们就会更加注重精细化和产品质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. I didn't know you do that. You actually go ahead and launch things really early to a select group of people that want the early stuff. Then, did you say that you find one customer to co-create and help evolve the feature and change it?
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。我不知道你们会这么做。你们实际上会很早地向一小群想要体验新功能的人推出产品。那么，你是说你们会找一个客户来共同开发并帮助改进功能吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Usually it can be one or it's three or five or 10. Often, especially with the larger company facing features, we usually do try to find a large company because sometimes it's hard to imagine these things, how they should work. It's better if someone is willing to work with us to explain, "Okay, this is how we do something." For example, we work this way with Vercel in that there was some changes they wanted to see in the roadmap feature. We worked with them to improve it and then they could give us feedback along the way.
turns.zh: 通常来说，可能是一个客户，也可能是三五个客户。尤其是面对大型公司提出的功能需求时，我们通常会尝试寻找大公司合作，因为有时很难想象这些功能应该如何运作。如果有人愿意与我们合作，解释说：“好的，我们应该这样做。”那就更好了。例如，我们与Vercel的合作就是如此，他们希望在路线图功能中看到一些改进。我们与他们合作进行改进，然后他们可以随时给我们反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting because I think people seeing Linear from the outside, it feels like you just take the time you need to build something awesome. Then, it launches and it's amazing and it's great, but it turns out that isn't exactly how you build. You actually do launch things really early and people don't necessarily see it until it's done, but there's this whole process behind the scenes.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣，因为我觉得从外部看Lineary的人会觉得，你们只需要花足够的时间打造出色的产品。然后产品上线后，效果惊艳、口碑极佳，但事实证明，产品的研发过程并非如此。你们实际上会很早地推出产品，用户往往要等到产品完成后才能看到背后的全貌。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think sometimes people think that craft is about perfecting things and perfecting them in a very organized way or very early on. The downside with this perfection mindset is that it can be sometimes hard to put anything out because nothing is ever fully perfect. We try to balance this thinking with the fact that we should be always pushing things out very quickly, but then also fixing them, improving them very quickly. (00:11:51): It's almost like the opposite idea, but then we try to combine that and I think it's been working well. Generally, in the company there's not necessarily a lot of reviews or something that we always review everything that gets shipped this way because we do want people to feel that they can put something in the app and then we can try it out. It's more like let's just try it out, but then we do need to look at it again before we release it to everyone.
turns.zh: 我认为有些人认为精益求精意味着要在很早的阶段就把事情做到尽善尽美。但这种完美主义思维模式的弊端在于，有时很难将成果推向市场，因为完美永远无法完全实现。我们试图平衡这种思维方式，既要快速推出产品，又要迅速修复和改进。（00:11:51）：这几乎是相反的理念，但我们努力将两者结合起来，我觉得效果不错。通常，在公司里没有太多评审环节，也不会对所有上线的产品进行全面审查，因为我们希望员工能有一种把产品投入应用后就能立即试用的感觉。更多时候是先快速试用，但在面向所有用户发布前还是需要再次评估。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of founders, a lot of product leaders, a lot of designers definitely want to create space for craft and making products really great, something they're really proud of, but in practice it's really hard. Very few teams and companies do this. Is there anything else you've learned about creating space for this sort of thing and prioritizing it for founders that are listening that are trying to instill more and more of this or do you have to be a designer CO like Karri and really it's hard to do otherwise?
turns.zh: 很多创始人、产品负责人、设计师都希望为精益求精留出空间，打造出令自己引以为傲的优质产品，但在实践中这实在不易。真正能做到这一点的团队和公司屈指可数。对于正在倾听的创始人，你们有没有什么关于如何为这种理念创造空间、优先推进的经验？或者说，你们必须得像Karri那样身兼设计总监之职，否则真的很难做到吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I don't think actually. It's not purely coming from me. I think all of us founders like Jori and Tuomas additionally, their background is engineering, but I would say I think they spend even more time on the details than sometimes I do. I think very early on when it was the three of us I would be the one doing the broad strokes designs like this is how the UI works and this is how some of the things work. They were the ones that were like, "Oh, there should be animation here and there should be this kind of thing here." (00:13:27): I think it's like that DNA I think comes from all of us. I think with the craft it always starts with people need to care about it. If it's not valued in the company, then it's very hard for anyone to do because people don't feel like it's valued. I gave this advice to some founder. He was asking me about it and in their case their founders were coming from different companies. Maybe this one founder came from Airbnb and then the other ones came from Facebook and Amazon. For example, I think Facebook and Amazon have a very different culture on quality or craft or shipping. I think it's what I said to them. You need to align on it. It's like you cannot run a company with multiple different kinds of cultures. I think I made some points like why the quality is important for certain products and you should all believe in that and then instill that with everyone you hire. The other thing I would say that we like to do is we actually don't have much PMs in the company. (00:14:32): We only have one and we can talk about more about it. One of the things I think that happens is when you build a team and you start creating these very specific roles for everything I think that often the PM can be the ones figuring things out and making decisions and guiding the team, but they're not the ones building the feature. They're not there looking at it the whole day like where does this button go or how does it work? I think a lot of that, this craft for us happens when we give the project team this ownership and the project team is just engineering and design. (00:15:11): Then, when they start building that feature they start seeing these opportunities that this thing could be better. A good example of this is one of our engineers, Andreas. When we were building this right click menu in the app so you can click different things and under that you have sub-menus. Mac OS does this well where it's when you open that menu you hover on the menu and then you want to go to the sub-menu. You hover to the right. You don't have to go exactly horizontally to get into that menu. (00:15:44): You can actually go diagonally or you don't actually have to hit the menu exactly. There's this safe zone, but a lot of software just implements like, "Hey, let's do this menu. Let's make the sub-menu." It only works if you exactly hover over the menu. Then, what happens is the user often misses with few pixels what they were trying to do. What Andreas did, which we didn't tell him to do, is like, "Yeah, this kind of sucks and we should make this better." (00:16:12): He figured out a way to create those safe areas that are dynamic based on the sub-menu positioning and everything. It's much easier now. You can go diagonally to the actual thing you want to go to. I think these things happen when you give people more of the ownership of the project and also the space to do that and then you also have leadership or generally the company culture that values the quality or the craft.
turns.zh:
我不这么认为。这不完全是我个人的想法。我觉得像乔里（Jori）和图奥马斯（Tuomas）这样的创始人，他们的背景都是工程师，但我认为他们在细节上投入的时间甚至比我还要多。在公司早期，只有我们三个人的时候，我会负责宏观设计，比如界面如何运作，某些功能如何实现。而他们会说，“这里应该加动画效果，那里应该调整布局。”（00:13:27）我认为这种对细节的执着是我们所有人的共同特质。说到工艺，首先要让团队成员重视它。如果公司内部不重视工艺，任何人都很难做到这一点，因为人们会觉得这不受重视。我曾给一些创始人建议，他们问我关于团队文化的问题。他们的创始人来自不同公司，比如一个来自Airbnb，另一个来自Facebook和亚马逊。我认为Facebook和亚马逊在质量、工艺和交付方面有着截然不同的文化。这就是我对他们的忠告——必须达成共识。一个公司不可能由多种不同文化共存。我还强调了质量对某些产品的重要性，所有人都要坚信这一点，并将其贯彻到每位新员工身上。  

另一个我们推崇的做法是，公司里几乎没有专门的项目经理（PM）。（00:14:32）我们只有一位PM，但可以再详细说说。当你组建团队时，如果为每个角色都设定固定职责，PM可能成为决策者、指导团队的人，但他们并非功能开发的主力军。他们不会整天盯着代码，思考按钮该放在哪里，功能如何运作。这些工艺细节往往是在赋予项目团队自主权后才体现出来的。  

例如，我们在应用中开发右键菜单时，参考了Mac OS的操作方式：当用户打开菜单时，鼠标悬停在菜单上即可进入子菜单。Mac OS的交互设计很巧妙，用户无需严格沿着水平线操作，可以斜向移动或通过悬停进入子菜单。但很多软件只实现了直线操作，导致用户经常因误操作而失败。安德烈亚斯（Andreas）主动改进，他发现现有菜单存在安全区域不足的问题，于是根据子菜单位置动态调整安全区域，现在用户可以斜向点击目标功能。  

这类创新源于赋予项目团队自主权，营造重视工艺的文化氛围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got to follow this thread. There's a couple of questions I want to ask. You have one product manager. Would you call him the head of product?
turns.zh: 我得跟进一下这个话题。我有几个问题想问。你们只有一位产品经理，你们会称他为产品负责人吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, Nan Yu, he is the head of product.
turns.zh: 是的，南宇，他就是产品负责人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, what made you decide to hire him and even have any PMs?
turns.zh: 太棒了，是什么让你们决定聘请他，甚至有产品经理这个职位？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: We started to see that we have enough features and areas of the product and also the team speaker that it's hard to keep aligned on all of these things or even keep track of things. Initially, we actually hired Nan as a contractor to help us with this insights data tool. We have this data tool feature built in Linear so you can get data on what's happening in the workspace. For us founders, we realized none of us, we are not super experienced in data tools. We need someone to help out. (00:17:34): Luckily, Nan, we knew him and he actually worked at Mode, which is a data tool. We initially hired him like, "Can you help us figure out what exactly should this data tool and how should it work?" I think there's different ways of doing that. I think always the easiest way is let's just copy what some other company is doing, but we didn't want to do that. We wanted to figure out what is actually a useful way to use this data or get this data? (00:18:01): He helped us with that and then we saw this could be useful in other larger areas or overall with the whole product it's like we might have these kind of questions. What should we exactly be thinking around here and why and how would we define this direction and then help the teams to also align on it? To us, it's more like he figures out the direction of the product and steers some of the efforts and not like he's there in every meeting and making every decision or writing every spec or something like that.
turns.zh: 我们开始意识到产品有足够多的功能和领域，加上团队成员众多，要想把所有这些事情协调一致，甚至跟踪进展变得很困难。最初，我们实际上是以合同工的形式聘请南宇来帮助我们开发这个洞察数据工具。我们在 Linear 中内置了这个数据工具功能，这样你就能获取工作区内发生的数据信息。对于我们这些创始人来说，我们意识到自己都不是数据工具方面的行家。我们需要有人来帮忙。（00:17:34）：幸运的是，南宇我们认识他，他之前在 Mode 公司工作，Mode 是一家数据工具公司。我们最初聘请他时问：“你能帮我们搞清楚这个数据工具应该是什么样的，应该如何运作吗？”我认为有不同的实现方式。最简单的办法就是照搬其他公司的做法，但我们不想这么做。我们想弄清楚如何有效地利用这些数据，或者获取这些数据？（00:18:01）：他在这方面帮了我们，然后我们发现这在其他更大领域或整个产品中都可能有用，比如我们可能会遇到这类问题：我们到底应该怎么思考？为什么要这么做？如何确定这个方向？然后帮助团队也达成一致。对我们来说，他更多的是规划产品方向，指导一些工作，而不是每次会议都参与决策、撰写每个需求文档之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another question along this line, because there's a lot of PMs listening that are going to be like, "Oh, shit, these guys don't need PMs or PM is over, product management dead." Just another question along these lines, somebody needs to do the work that a PM does basically, right? There's all these things that is on the plate of a product manager when they're at a company and if they're not there, other people have to do those things. What I'm hearing is basically you give those responsibilities to the engineers, designer, and maybe other functions within the team. Is that right?
turns.zh: 再问一个相关的问题，因为有很多产品经理听了会觉得：“天哪，这些人不需要产品经理了，产品管理已经过时了。”再问一个类似的问题，基本上还是需要有人来承担产品经理的工作，对吧？产品经理在公司里要负责很多事情，如果没有产品经理，其他人就得做这些事。我听你们说基本上是把这些职责分给了工程师、设计师以及团队中的其他职能部门。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I mean definitely I think what it means is, and there's definitely a trade-off. I think sometimes when companies specialize roles a lot it's because it's more efficient. If the engineer spends 100% of their time coding something, then it's like they're using their skillset to the max. Then, we just think that in order to build quality things or build things in a certain way it's actually better if people actually also spend some time thinking about things and not just executing. (00:19:35): Yes, for every project there's a project lead. That lead can be engineer or designer. It's not a formal role or it's not based on your whatever level or it's just like you need to be certain title that you can be that. It's more like an assignment that now you are responsible getting the project started and working together with the team, figuring it out, and then communicating changes or communicating how that progress happens. (00:20:06): Definitely it means that the engineers or designers also have to do these things and they do need to communicate and they do need to think about the scope or things. It's a different way of doing things. Also, not everyone wants to do that, which is fine, but we on the hiring front try to hire people that are interested in the broader scope than just the specific skillset that they have.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认为这意味着——而且肯定存在权衡取舍。我觉得有时候公司把角色高度专业化，是因为这样更高效。如果工程师把100%的时间都花在编码上，那就是在最大限度地发挥他们的技能。但我们认为，要想打造高质量的产品或以特定方式开展工作，人们最好能抽出时间思考问题，而不只是执行任务。（00:19:35）：是的，每个项目都有项目负责人。这个角色可以是工程师或设计师。它不是一个正式职位，也不基于你的职级高低——你只需要具备某种头衔就能胜任。更像是一个临时任务，现在你负责启动项目，与团队合作，理清思路，然后沟通变更或汇报进展情况。（00:20:06）：这确实意味着工程师或设计师也需要做这些事情，他们确实需要沟通，也需要考虑项目范围等问题。这种工作方式有所不同。当然，不是每个人都愿意这么做，这没关系，但我们在招聘时会尽力招募那些对更广泛的项目视野感兴趣，而不只是局限于自身专业技能的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think those last two points are really essential. One, people often don't want to do this work and they are happy to offload it to a potential product manager. The fact that say engineers have to do all these boring PM things like communicate timelines and keep PR specs aligned and make sure timelines are hit and all that stuff and run meetings, a lot of people don't want to do that. (00:20:57): A lot of times they do and I think in this case people seem to really want to be doing that. The other is I think you need a really high caliber team that's very product-minded and the hiring bar needs to be very, very high for say engineers and designers to want to do all these things and be good at them. I think those are two necessary ingredients for this to work out.
turns.zh: 我认为最后两点非常重要。一是人们往往不愿意做这些工作，乐于把这些任务推给潜在的产品经理。比如工程师不得不做那些无聊的产品经理工作，比如沟通时间表、确保PR规范一致、确保时间表按时完成、主持会议等等，很多人都不愿意做这些事。（00:20:57）：很多时候他们确实这么做了，而且我觉得在这种情况下，人们似乎真的很愿意做这些事。另一个是，我认为你需要一个高水平、极具产品思维的团队，招聘门槛必须非常非常高，这样工程师和设计师才会愿意做这些事情并做好它们。我认为这是成功实施这种模式的两个必要条件。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For teams that want to try this approach, especially startups that are starting out and maybe not excited about hiring product managers, is there anything else that you think is essential or important to functioning well without any product managers? You're at around 50 people at this point?
turns.zh: 对于想尝试这种方法的团队，特别是初创公司，可能不急于招聘产品经理，还有什么你认为对没有产品经理的情况下良好运作至关重要的因素吗？你们现在大约有50人吧？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: We're around 50. Probably the only thing I would say is it's the hiring front that you really need to spend more time on it. Basically, you cannot really interview engineers only for the engineering skills. You also have to interview them for the product skills. Obviously, you cannot I think expect that people have some. If you do some PM interview for them, they're not going to have the same skillset or the same understanding of the concepts or something. (00:21:59): The way we have done it in the past is basically I might interview them about the product. I'm not a technical person per se. I will just ask them questions about how did they do something or how do they think about something? It's similar to other roles too. We just look for does this person have opinions about products and how they work? Can they form opinions and can they use their own judgment at times? Then, can they communicate or articulate those things as well?
turns.zh: 我们大约有50人。唯一我想说的是，招聘时你真的需要花更多时间在工程师身上，不仅要看他们的工程技能，还要看他们的产品技能。显然，你不能期望人们天生就具备这些技能。如果你对他们进行产品经理面试，他们不会有相同的技能组合或对概念的理解之类的。（00:21:59）：我们过去的做法基本上是，我可能会面试他们关于产品方面的问题。我本身不是技术人员。我会问他们一些问题，比如他们是如何做某件事的，或者他们如何看待某件事？这对其他角色来说也类似。我们就是寻找这个人对产品及其运作方式是否有见解？他们能否形成观点，有时能否运用自己的判断力？然后，他们能否沟通或清晰表达这些想法？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, I was just thinking it's interesting that a tool that, I don't think it's designed specifically for product managers, but essentially for building products like the infrastructure for building product in a team is built by a company that has one PM and very few PMs.
turns.zh: 太棒了，我刚刚在想，虽然Linear这款工具并非专为产品经理设计，但本质上是为团队构建产品基础设施而打造的，而它的开发公司却只有一位产品经理和极少的PM团队。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I mean I think in some ways I would say that with Linear we're trying to help the whole company and I think engineers is probably the largest user group of the product. I think in some ways we want to make the PM's job easier in that they have to spend less time managing everything or the day-to-day because the engineers are actually using the product and they're updating the things. For the PMs, it would be much more easier to get what is the state of things and maybe trust that much more because people actually use the product. (00:23:18): In some ways, I think we are trying to make it easier for everyone, easier for the engineers. They can focus more on their work. Then, for PMs I think we're trying to make it so that they can also focus more on other things than just, I don't know, managing the tool that they use. I think that's not the most important job of a PM. I think they should be thinking more of the, I don't know, bigger picture or the other problems or figuring out the next features or something.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，我认为从某种角度来说，我们借助Linear正努力为整个公司提供支持，而工程师群体或许是该产品最大的用户群体。我们希望通过这款产品，让PM们的工作更轻松——他们无需耗费大量时间管理日常事务，因为工程师们会主动使用产品并进行更新。此时，PM们就能更清晰地掌握项目进展，也能更放心地信任产品实际运行的效果。
（00:23:18）：从某种角度看，我们正努力让一切变得更简单，让工程师们能更专注于核心工作。对于PM们而言，我们希望他们也能将精力投入到更宏观的层面，比如思考更深远的战略问题、攻克其他难题、规划新功能等，而这些才是PM最重要的职责所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just one more question along these lines, there's other companies like Stripe I think waited until 200 employees to hire I think their first product manager. Snapchat I think is famous for something around that. Do you have any sense of if you think this might change, when you think you might hire more product managers? Is there a plan here or is it just see how it goes as you grow?
turns.zh: 再问一个相关问题，我记得像Stripe这样的公司直到员工规模达到200人后才聘请首位产品经理。Snapchat因类似情况而闻名。您认为这种情况会否有所改变？何时会考虑增加PM数量？是否有相关规划，还是会顺其自然？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think we'll definitely hire more. It's I think like what I said before. I think we like to see the PM's smarts operating on a higher level. The whole company, I think the way we are trying to build it is we have less people, but people who are more high caliber and can think about larger scope than what their current role is. (00:24:29): I think we're just trying to build smaller units, but more effective units, which is I think where the PMs go. There would be also less of them and they're not there at every level. I think in the future as the company grows and the team grows and the product grows, we might have several PMs that are focusing on or looking at specific areas or specific types of things of the product or specific customers or something like that.
turns.zh: 我们肯定会继续增加PM数量。正如我之前所说，我希望看到PM们能在更高层面发挥智慧。就整个公司而言，我们正致力于打造精简高效的团队，PM们将成为其中的核心力量。他们将不再遍布各个层级，而是专注于特定领域或产品类型、特定客户群体等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, that was a tangent because I could not go in that direction, but I want to come back to design again and craft.
turns.zh: 太棒了，刚才有点跑题了，但我想再回到设计与创新的话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... not go in that direction, but I want to come back to design again and craft. So it feels like Linear, one of the reasons you guys have been successful is design and experience is basically a huge differentiator from other products and there's always this question of can design be enough of a differentiator in specific markets? Is there always an opportunity to build a significantly better product experience and have a real shot at disrupting an incumbent? Do you have any sense of when design can be enough of a differentiator? And this is coming from a founder trend aside, should we go big on design and experience or should we invest in distribution or new technology or something along those lines? Any thoughts there?
turns.zh: ……不过我想再回到设计与创新的话题。就Linear而言，你们能取得成功的核心原因之一在于设计和用户体验，这与其他产品形成了显著差异。人们总会质疑：设计能否在特定市场中成为核心差异化因素？是否存在打造显著优于竞争对手的产品体验、真正颠覆现有巨头的机遇？您对设计何时能成为核心差异化因素有何见解？暂且抛开创始人思维，面对这样的挑战，我们是该在设计与体验上大下血本，还是优先投入分销、技术创新等领域？您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: My belief is that any domain or industry, the more it matters, the more the design matters. I think it's fairly easy to see in different, even in software or in other industries. It's like what happens is whenever there's a new paradigm, I don't know, it's the mobile or the web or something, the first iterations of those products existing there, they don't have to be super well-designed necessarily because they're the first. But then as you build the hundreds, thousand different email clients, any email client now has to be pretty good to be even considered an email client. The bar is so high. (00:26:23): I think today the startups, I don't know if you look at the webpage Google launched with or the webpage YouTube launched with or some of these older companies, they were very basic. If you launch that website today, no one would really pay attention. So I think the design is, it's almost like a very basic thing now, that from pretty much from the very beginning you need pretty high level design for people to even pay attention or consider you seriously. (00:26:56): And I think it's not necessarily fair because sometimes it's like maybe the product is really good but they didn't have a designer or they didn't have time to do it and then people just dismiss it because it doesn't seem like something that they interest them. So I think that's the first thing is I think it is, and it's going to be more and more important. But I would also say design is never going to be the reason why a company is successful. It's like the company still has to have some other things. The product still needs to be something, it needs to be better in some ways or it needs to be different in some ways. (00:27:36): And then a design is just enabling some of these things, enable and similar to technology, it's like if you have good technology, it's easier to do certain things and the product works better in some ways than you having a bad technology or bad infrastructure. (00:27:53): So similar to design, I think if you have a good design or even a good brand, people are drawn into it and then it makes some user acquisition or user retention or just even people perception of the product better. I think an example is packaging and products, is like Apple or a lot of companies spend a lot of time effort into the packaging because it's kind of already sets the expectations for the user who is receiving the product. It's like even before you use the product, you start thinking that this is a high quality product and I'm going to love it. And then when you actually have it, then you actually might feel that way, unless the product is really bad and then you wouldn't feel that way. (00:28:40): So I think similarly, with startups or SaaS, it's like your landing page or some of the other things. It's like they are already communicating something to the user and they're setting the expectations and then I think that that can be very useful thing, especially early on when no one really knows you or knows the product or cares about you. So I think especially, I feel like design can be very good leverage in the beginning.
turns.zh:
我认为，在任何领域或行业中，越是重要，设计就越重要。这一点在不同领域，甚至在软件或其他行业中都相当明显。比如，当出现新的范式时，比如移动互联网或Web技术，早期产品的迭代版本不一定需要精心设计，因为它们是开创性的。但当产品数量达到数百、数千个时，每个邮件客户端都必须足够优秀才能被视为合格的邮件客户端。标准门槛被大幅提高了。（00:26:23）：我觉得如今的初创公司——无论是谷歌刚推出的网页、YouTube的首页，还是一些老牌公司——它们最初的页面都非常简陋。如果你现在推出这样的网站，没人会真正关注。所以我认为设计现在几乎成了一个基础要素，从一开始就需要高水平的设计才能让用户注意到你、认真考虑你。
（00:26:56）：但我觉得这并不公平，有时候产品可能很棒，但他们没有设计师或没有时间做设计，然后人们就否定它，因为它看起来不符合他们的兴趣。所以我认为第一点是，设计现在很重要，而且会越来越重要。但我也要说，设计永远不是公司成功的唯一原因。公司还需要其他东西。产品必须有优势，或在某些方面与众不同。
（00:27:36）：设计就像技术一样。好技术能让某些事情更容易实现，产品也能因此表现得更好。反之，糟糕的技术或基础设施会拖后腿。
（00:27:53）：设计同样重要。苹果或许多公司在产品包装上投入大量心血，因为这能为用户设定预期。用户还没用产品时，就觉得这是一款高质量的产品，会喜欢它。实际使用后，如果产品确实出色，用户就会有同样的感受；反之则不会。
（00:28:40）：初创公司或SaaS产品也是如此，比如登录页面等。这些设计都在向用户传递信息，设定预期。这在初期尤其有用，尤其是当没人了解你、产品或在乎你的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such an interesting insight, especially that first thing you said around how the more often and the more crowded the spaces, the more opportunity there is for design to be a differentiator. Is that roughly how you think about it?
turns.zh: 我觉得这真是个有趣的见解，尤其是你说的第一点——越是竞争激烈、市场拥挤，设计就越能成为差异化因素。您大致是这么理解的吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. So I mean just think about, I don't know, any product category, basically people have then a lot of choices and then they how do they make choices? Maybe there's a specific thing they want, but a lot of people don't necessarily know what is the specific feature I want from this software. So it's more like, well what is the best one? What is the highest quality one? And if you put things side by side and people see things, people are visual. So then the design can be one of those things, it stands out, it's like, "Well, that looks the best or that looks the most quality product to me, so I'm going to use that one." When people have a lot of choices, they probably will pick the one that looks most interesting. (00:30:04): Then I think there is, the second part is the brand, which is something that if you can build a brand, then I think it's even the product almost doesn't matter, it becomes this kind of default. I don't know again, like Apple or Nike, it's like yeah, there's all kinds of shoes you can buy, but there's a reason for someone to buy Nike shoes other than some random brand. Even if the random brand would be actually a better shoe, they still buy Nike because they, I don't know, like the brand. So then I think both the design of the product but also the design of the brand can be very strong things that pull people to your company or to the product.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我想说，你可以想想，任何产品类别中，人们都有很多选择，但他们该如何做出选择呢？也许他们有特定的需求，但很多人并不清楚自己真正想从这款软件中获得什么功能。所以更多时候，他们会问：“哪个是最好的？”“哪个质量最高？”当你把产品并排展示时，人们会被视觉效果吸引。因此，设计可能成为关键因素——它能脱颖而出，比如“嗯，这个看起来最棒，或者这个产品看起来质量最高，所以我要用它。” 当人们面临众多选择时，他们很可能会选择看起来最有趣的那一个。（00:30:04）：然后我认为第二个要素是品牌。如果你能成功打造品牌，那么产品本身几乎就不重要了，它会成为一种默认选择。我不知道，比如苹果或耐克，虽然市面上有各种鞋子可供选择，但人们选择耐克鞋的原因不只是因为它是随机品牌。即使其他品牌的鞋子质量更好，人们还是会选择耐克，因为他们喜欢这个品牌。所以我认为产品设计和品牌设计都是能吸引用户的重要因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you've learned about just building a brand over the course of building Linear, something you find to be really important in actually building that perception that Linear is really great and amazing
turns.zh: 在构建Linear的过程中，你有没有学到什么关于品牌建设的经验？对于让人们认为Linear真的很棒、很出色，有什么关键要素？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: To me, I think the brand should be always authentic and it should, I think even if people can't articulate it, if people start to feel like something is off, I think there can be companies or startups, they think about brands like, oh brand is the logo or the colors of the website or something. And then they do the same thing and some other company does and then they think, "Okay, now we have a brand." But you actually didn't think about what's your brand, what is the message or voice you want to talk about? And it doesn't also, the brand doesn't happen overnight. (00:31:34): So it's basically just you start in the beginning and when you start a company you don't have no brand and so you have to create it and you create it over time by the things you do, the things you say, how you say them and how do you approach things, how do you treat customers, how do you build the website or the product? All of these things starts to build this idea, what does this company mean to me in people's heads? (00:32:02): I know we both worked at Airbnb and I think Brian Chesky is, I think the brand was probably the most important thing for him. And I don't know how many hours or meetings or conversations there was about the brand and the brand was always, it's part of everything the company does. Because it's true. It's like, yeah, you could book things like places to stay in a lot of places on the web, but when people think about, "Oh, I want to stay in some cool place," they're going to think about Airbnb. It's like they're not going to think about those other places. So that's the power of the brand, people stop thinking about the other things or they start understanding, okay, this is the thing for this.
turns.zh: 对我来说，品牌应该始终保持真实。即使人们无法清晰表达品牌理念，如果他们开始觉得哪里不对劲，我认为有些公司或初创企业会把品牌想得太简单，比如认为品牌就是标志或网站配色之类的。然后他们照搬其他公司的做法，却自以为这就是品牌。但实际上，你从未真正思考过品牌的本质——你想传达什么样的信息和声音？品牌也不是一夜之间就能形成的。（00:31:34）：所以基本上，在创立公司之初，你没有品牌，所以必须亲手打造它。通过你的行动、言语、沟通方式、对待客户的态度，以及产品和网站的建设，品牌会逐渐在人们心目中形成印象——这家公司对我意味着什么？（00:32:02）：我知道我们都曾在Airbnb工作过，我认为布莱恩·切斯基（Brian Chesky）把品牌视为最重要的战略方向。我不知道团队花了多少时间讨论品牌，但品牌始终渗透在公司运营的方方面面。因为事实就是如此。比如，人们可以在网上预订很多住宿，但当人们想到“我想住在一个很酷的地方”时，首先想到的还是Airbnb，而不是其他平台。这就是品牌的力量——人们会自动排除其他选项，或者明白“这就是我要找的”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's part of the reason Airbnb's been able to build a direct destination where people aren't Googling, I want to stay in a home. They're like airbnb.com, which gives Airbnb such a massive advantage not having to run ads on Facebook and Google or SEO. It's just like people know Airbnb and they just go straight there. And there's very few sites where people go, "I'm going to go straight there and look for some," knowing that they can also compare hotels on all these other sites. (00:33:08): Coming back to design briefly, just very practically, how do you guys do design reviews? Just how do you actually go about reviewing what's going at, and then this may be too big a question, but just whatever you can share here, is just how do you know when it's done? How do you know when it's ready and approved? Karri sealed, checkbox, ready to go.
turns.zh:
这一点也是Airbnb能够打造直接预订平台的原因所在——用户无需在谷歌上搜索“我想住在别人家”之类的关键词。Airbnb官网就是这样一个直接预订平台，这让Airbnb在无需在Facebook和谷歌投放广告、无需进行SEO优化的情况下占据了巨大优势。用户直接访问Airbnb.com就能找到心仪的房源，而很少有其他平台能让用户一想到住宿就直接想到Airbnb。相反，用户在其他平台寻找住宿时，通常会先货比三家。

（00:33:08）回到设计环节，简单说一下实际操作流程。你们是如何进行设计评审的？具体来说，如何评估设计进展？或许这个问题太宏大了，但如果方便的话，能否分享一下，你们是如何判断设计完成的？如何确定设计稿最终定稿并获得批准？卡里·西尔（Karri Seal）勾选了相关选项，表示设计工作已完成，可以正式上线了。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: We've been exploring different ways of doing this. I think today, I still run the design team, so I do see some of the designs on a weekly basis and then, or one of the other co-founders or head of product, we are basically the sponsors for the projects. So then we are responsible reviewing the work. And so we might just have a meeting where we go through, okay, well let's go through the demo and people can explain what's going on and how they think about it and why. And then we might have feedback, okay, this seems strange or something, and then just after that I might just go into the product myself and try it out. And then what happens sometimes, it's in the initial stages, obviously we're not going to start fixing everything, it's just more like let's try to get the main concept there and figure out how it works. (00:34:27): But then before we are launching it, I might just go in and try it out and try the different states and click it around. And sometimes I find things, like we were building this threading to comments and then when it looked all good in the demos and stuff, and then I went to try it and try different lengths of messages and stuff and then I start to see, oh, sometimes the animations are kind of janky or it's just off. They don't go the right way, the screen doesn't scroll exactly right. So then I just captured those things and send it to the team. And so we had to pull back the release a little bit until those things were fixed. That one was, it's very, I think a simple concept and it's very known concept like, okay, this is how threading comments works. So that was mostly about, okay, what's the execution of this? (00:35:22): But then we have projects where we are not sure exactly how this should work and we can try it ourselves. We also have to see how companies use it. So something like we built this feature project updates and it's a common thing companies do. It's like you need to write an update on a project. Is it yellow, green, red? And companies have very different ways of doing this in different tools and we just thought, well, I think it would be really nice if it's inside Linear and the team, when they work on a project, they can write the update, Linear can also capture some of the stats, what actually happened. I think with that feature it's been working well, but then also now it'd be exploring. It's like after using it a while we think, oh actually, if there could be more robust way of following these updates. Maybe the leadership could just get these updates over email or maybe when you have a lot of updates you should have a search or a filtering system or something. So I think a lot of times we just think, okay, this is the scope of it for now and we are okay launching this and the execution is good. But we know that this is not the fully figured out version and we just need to see people trying it out and see the feedback.
turns.zh:
我们一直在探索不同的实现方式。我觉得如今，我仍负责设计团队的工作，所以我每周都会审阅一些设计方案。然后，或者由其他联合创始人或产品负责人来负责，这些人基本上就是项目的发起人。因此，我们有责任对工作成果进行审查。例如，我们可能会召开会议，仔细审查演示内容，让相关人员解释设计思路和逻辑。之后，我们会提出反馈意见，比如“这部分看起来不太自然”之类的。接着，我可能会亲自试用产品，体验不同状态下的操作。有时在项目初期，我们不会急于修复所有问题，而是专注于搭建核心概念并验证其可行性。

（00:34:27）但在产品上线前，我会亲自测试，检查不同状态下的交互效果，比如评论的分层机制。尽管演示版本看起来没问题，但实际试用时，我会发现动画卡顿、页面滚动不流畅等问题。这些问题被记录后反馈给团队，最终导致发布计划被推迟。这类问题通常源于简单但常见的概念，比如评论分层机制。接下来是执行层面的考量：如何将这个功能落地？

（00:35:22）还有些项目，我们不确定具体实现方式，就需要亲自测试。此外，我们还要观察企业用户的使用场景。例如，我们开发的项目更新功能，是企业常用功能。用户需要为项目撰写更新日志，但不同工具的呈现方式差异巨大。我们设想，如果能在 Linear 中实现团队协作时，让成员直接撰写更新日志，并同步更新数据统计，将非常有用。目前该功能运行良好，但我们仍在探索改进空间，比如让管理层通过邮件接收更新通知，或者为海量更新添加搜索与筛选功能。很多时候，我们会权衡当前版本的成熟度和用户反馈，再决定是否上线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like on the decision of whether it goes out or not, it's kind of this intuitive feeling from your actual experience trying it out, feeling gut level, this is ready or this needs a little work?
turns.zh: 所以在决定是否上线时，更多是基于亲身试用后的直觉判断，凭感觉判断它是否准备就绪，还是需要进一步打磨？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I would say a lot of things that we do is more like that but we don't do AP testing or we don't do specific, go follow certain metrics or something. Sometimes we do have telemetry or we can look at how people use certain things and we sometimes do that, but that's not usually the goal we have in mind, like, yeah, we should move this number this much. So it's more about based on the understanding of the problem we have and based on the [inaudible 00:37:16], what we think is right, is this the right solution and is this a good enough solution to be released to the customers?
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得我们做的很多事情都类似于此，但我们不进行AP测试，也不专注于特定指标之类的。有时候我们会用遥测数据观察用户使用某项功能的情况，但这通常不是我们的核心目标——比如，‘我们应该把这个数据提升到多少’之类的。所以更多时候，我们是基于对问题的理解，以及基于[听不清 00:37:16]的判断，思考这是否是正确的解决方案，是否值得向客户发布？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One more question along this thread is how do you actually structure these reviews? It sounds like you go straight to a prototype. Is there a design review phase? Is it all kind of informal and people just review, here's what we need your feedback on?
turns.zh: 关于这个话题的另一个问题是，你们是如何组织这些评审的？听起来你们直接就进入原型阶段了。那有没有设计评审阶段呢？还是说整个过程比较随意，大家只是看看产品，问问意见？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So projects don't necessarily have specific states to them, but I would say roughly, usually we do start with design. So there's some explorations on the design, there's different ways that we could approach this or sometimes there's just one way because pretty clear. But then what I said before, is that we do try to get into the building phase as quickly as possible because then we can also see is this direction actually reasonable and is there some problems it causes or how does it just generally feel here? So I think that there isn't specific review stages. It's more like, yeah, let's check on this project every week or every two weeks and then before releasing, let's also make a review of it and really test it out, is it the quality we want?
turns.zh: 所以项目通常没有特定的阶段，但大致来说，我们确实从设计开始。会对设计进行探索，思考可以采用哪些方法，有时也会因为思路清晰而直接采用某种方案。但正如我之前说的，我们会尽快进入构建阶段，这样就能判断这个方向是否合理，是否会带来问题，以及整体体验如何。所以我觉得没有特定的评审阶段。更多的是每周或两周对项目进行检查，然后在发布前再做一次全面评审，真正测试产品是否达到了我们期望的质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So that's a good segue to another area I wanted to spend some time, which is the Linear Method. You espouse this way of building product that you call the Linear Method, which you publish online and willing to in the show notes. And I just want to ask a few questions around this way of building product. One is, you are big on this idea of building opinionated software. Can you talk about just what does that mean and then maybe give an example or two of how you actually have done that at Linear?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这正好可以过渡到我接下来想探讨的另一个领域——线性方法。你倡导一种叫做“线性方法”的产品开发思路，还把它发布到了网上，并愿意在节目笔记中分享。我想就这种产品开发方式提几个问题。首先，你非常强调构建有主见的软件。能否解释一下这个概念的含义，再举一两个例子说明在Lineary是如何做到的？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So first with the Linear Method, why did we create it in the first place? Is we just believe that there is more of this modern ways of building software and thinking about it. And we wanted to share some of our thinking on it. And that's also, it relates to how we built Linear as well. So you might understand why we make some choices because this is the way we think about making these choices. So we are trying to share our thinking behind the product and also just like, here's the product and figure it out. (00:39:33): So the opinionated piece, I personally have this belief that productivity software should be, and especially company software should be opinionated. I think that what the productivity software is trying to do is make people productive. And I think what productive means is you actually do something that matters for the company, which is, I don't know, build some new feature or fix something or design something. (00:40:02): All of those things are eventually, they provide some kind of value for the customer. I think there is this ideas or notions in the world that flexible software is great. I'm like, I think it can be great sometimes. But what happens is people start spending a lot of time figuring things out. Like, how does this feature work? You can use it in 10 different ways and then every team or everyone figures out the different way of doing it. (00:40:27): So our thinking is we like to provide this good default or good opinions. Like, this is how the feature works and this is how the workflow works. So you, as a user or as a team don't have to think about it and you can focus on the work you do. And the other thing is, my design mantra is always design something for someone. It is very hard to design everything for everyone because you just end up with a very generalized solution. So then what we are trying to do with the opinionated solution is that that's the best solution or at the most optimized solution we think of. (00:41:06): And then when you use it, hopefully you agree and you can feel that it's most optimized. So being opinionated, I think the value it provides people is you don't have to think too much or spend more time on the tool than you do on your actual work.
turns.zh: 接下来是线性方法（Linear Method）。我们最初为什么要开发它？是因为我们坚信现代软件开发和思维方式正在发生深刻变革，我们希望分享自己的见解。这也与我们构建Lineary平台的理念息息相关。通过分享产品背后的设计思路，我们希望让用户能更清晰地理解我们的决策逻辑。（00:39:33）关于产品设计的观点，个人认为生产力软件，尤其是企业级软件，应该具备明确的指导性设计。生产力软件的核心价值在于帮助用户为公司创造实际价值，比如开发新功能、修复漏洞、进行设计等，最终为客户创造价值。（00:40:02）当前，市场上存在着灵活性至上的观点。我认为灵活性有其价值，但过度灵活会导致用户花费大量时间摸索功能细节。例如，某个功能有十种实现方式，每个团队都可能采用不同的实现方案。（00:40:27）我们的设计理念是提供清晰的默认配置和最佳实践，明确功能逻辑和工作流程，让用户专注于核心任务。此外，我的设计准则始终是“为特定场景设计”。试图迎合所有人的需求最终只能得到一个通用化的解决方案。因此，我们推行指导性设计，力求提供最优解方案。（00:41:06）用户使用后，若能认同并感受到其高效性，这就是设计的价值所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then another core element of the Linear Method is something you call cycles. I know Linear is all around this idea of creating cycles and working in cycles. Can you talk about what is a cycle and how it works at Linear?
turns.zh: 接下来是线性方法的核心要素——循环周期（cycles）。Lineary始终围绕创建循环和循环式工作展开。能否解释一下循环周期是什么，以及它在Lineary中的具体应用？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So for example, the cycles, it's optional, not that the whole team has to use it or not that the whole company has to use it, but it's there as you can turn it on or off. But basically, I think why we created cycles is that I think any team that works on software or some other products, you always have almost infinite list of things to do and that list gets longer every day. And it can be sometimes very distracting for the individual or for the team to decide, there's a new thing coming in, should we work on that or should we work on this other thing we decided in the past? So the cycles is just a way to say that for the next week or the next two weeks or whatever timeframe, we are going to work on these things and these other things we think are the priority or the focus for this timeframe. (00:42:27): And then the team can try to focus on those things. Now if something happens, like I don't know, we really need to jump on this other thing. At least there was some kind of initial state that we decided before we want to do these things and then now something else happened and so now we have to go on this thing. So you have an answer when someone comes to you to ask, "Why didn't you do this other thing before?" Then you can say, "Well, we did decide to do that, but then something happened and we had to do this other thing." (00:42:56): So the cycles, it's very similar to sprints, but we like to call it cycles because we are not really sprinting anywhere. The cycles also run on automated schedule. So it's like you don't have to think about which day does it start? Or every time, set it up manually so it just runs automatically. And so it's just meant to help the team to focus on, let's just focus on this few things and forget about the infinite list of other things that are in the background.
turns.zh: 比如说，周期机制是可选的。并非要求整个团队必须使用它，也不是强制整个公司必须采用，但用户可以根据需要启用或关闭该功能。不过，我认为我们创建周期机制的主要原因在于，任何从事软件或其他产品开发的团队，几乎都会面临无穷无尽的待办事项清单，而且这份清单每天都在不断增长。有时，个别成员或整个团队需要做出抉择：新任务来了——我们是该专注于这个，还是继续推进之前确定的其他任务？周期机制的核心在于：在接下来的一周、两周或任意设定的时间段内，我们将专注于这些任务，以及我们认为在该时间段内优先级最高的其他事项。（00:42:27）这样一来，团队就能集中精力完成既定任务。当然，如果出现突发情况，比如某个紧急任务需要立即处理，我们也会有初始的决策依据。这样当有人追问“为什么之前没处理那个任务？”时，团队就能回应：“我们确实计划处理那个任务，但临时有事不得不优先处理其他任务。”（00:42:56）周期机制与敏捷开发中的“冲刺周期”（sprints）非常相似，但我们更倾向于称之为“周期”，因为我们并非真的在某个特定阶段“冲刺”。周期机制会自动运行，无需手动设置启动时间。这样一来，团队就能专注于当前的任务，而无需被后台堆积如山的待办事项所干扰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned earlier that you don't set metrics goals and so let me dig into that a little bit. Is that true? You don't really have number goals for features for launches and things like that? And so let me start there and then I have a follow-up question.
turns.zh: 你之前提到不设定指标目标，我想深入探讨一下这个问题。是这样吗？你们确实没有针对功能发布等项目设定具体的数字目标吗？让我先从这个问题入手，然后再追问其他问题。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So we might have a company level goal sometimes, for example, weekly active users, that's a metric we want to increase or something. But in terms of specific features, we don't have goals for those. And the reason is that I think a product like us or a system that is used by different kinds of companies, and it's like a system made of multiple different parts and it's not necessarily like you want to optimize any specific thing about it. Also, companies are a little bit different, so their usage of different features can differ because they just operate slightly differently or their team size is different or the setup of the team is different or the culture is different. (00:44:27): So I think for example, I don't know, some Instagram or some of these apps, it's like, yeah, we need to drive engagement and that's the main feature. That's the main metric for every feature. We don't actually have that. We just think that there should be features that help companies and sometimes we can look at the metrics before we start working on it, like let's see what this state of things are, but we don't necessarily want to set, oh, we need to increase this specific metric by X. It's more like we want to solve this problem. And ideally, the success what it looks like customers agree that the problem is solved or they enjoy the solution and it's not like that the metrics went up.
turns.zh: 因此，有时我们可能会有公司层面的目标，比如每周活跃用户数，这是一个我们希望提升的指标。但对于具体的功能特性，我们并没有设定目标。原因在于，我认为像我们这样的产品，或者说一个被不同类型公司使用的系统，往往由多个不同模块组成，不一定需要对某个特定功能进行优化。此外，各家公司的需求差异较大，他们对不同功能的使用习惯可能因运营方式不同、团队规模不同、团队架构不同或文化差异而有所差异。（00:44:27） 比如，我不知道，Instagram或其他类似应用会设定目标，提升用户参与度是主要诉求，每个功能的核心指标都是用户活跃度。但我们没有这样的要求。我们只是认为应该开发能帮助企业的功能，有时在开始开发前会看看现有数据，比如用户使用情况如何，但我们不会设定具体的提升指标。我们的目标是解决实际问题，最终用户认可问题得到解决，或者对解决方案感到满意，而不只是看数据是否增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to summarize so far, you have no metrics, you have no experiments, you have essentially no PMs, just one product leader. You spend a lot of time on design and craft and making things awesome. I'm curious just what you think it takes to make a company work in that way? Because this is pretty different from how a lot of other founders think and a lot of other product teams work.
turns.zh: 总结一下，目前你们没有指标，没有实验，几乎没有产品经理，只有位产品负责人。你们把大量时间投入设计、打磨细节，致力于打造卓越的产品。我很好奇，要让一家公司以这种方式运作，需要具备哪些条件？因为这与许多其他创始人的理念和产品团队的运作方式大相径庭。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: We like to talk about this internally, I like this mixture of magic and science and how we described, there's always some level of science that we do. And I think some companies are very scientific on their product management that they like to measure everything and they do a lot of tests and things, but we just decided we don't think that's necessary or that's good for us. So the science for us, means that we do talk to users a lot and any project we start with, we do some level of user research and as founders, different people on the team, we might have weekly calls with customers or users. We also encourage everyone in the team, go to the customer Slack, they answer people questions. We have shared Slack channels with customers. Anyone, I sometimes go answer the questions there. I also see when they complain about something. I think the first part is the whole team has to be really understanding the product and the customers and the problems people are facing and have that empathy and as well as the understanding what is the state of things today. (00:46:47): And then we talk about that. And then sometimes we might pull up stats and see, oh, wonder, is there some kind of patterns we see, okay, these kind of companies are using this thing more and what do we think about it? But usually we have some kind of question we want to answer. It's like, I wonder what is going on. And then we look at it versus let's pull some metrics and then decide that we should increase this metric. And then the magic part is what happens when you build this understanding, everyone in the company builds. It's not like everyone has the same understanding, but everyone builds more of that customer and product understanding. Then we have discussions like what should we be doing or what decision we want to make here? Then everyone is much more informed of actual reality of the customers or the product. (00:47:40): And then we think you can much more use your intuition or thinking to do those decisions so you don't have to use data or metrics to back those things up. So I think the main thing is the whole company has to be with the customers or talk to them and then understand where the product might work well or where it might fall short.
turns.zh: 内部我们常谈论这个话题。我喜欢将魔法与科学相融合的方式，我们所描述的场景中始终存在着一定的科学成分。有些公司在产品管理上非常依赖数据科学，他们喜欢对一切进行量化测试，但我们认为这对我们来说既没必要也不见得有益。因此，对我们而言，科学意味着要经常与用户沟通。无论开展何种项目，我们都会进行一定程度的用户研究。作为创始人，团队中的不同成员每周都会与客户或用户进行电话沟通。我们还鼓励团队成员加入客户的Slack群组，回答用户提问，并与客户共享Slack频道。有时我也会亲自回复用户的投诉。我认为首要任务是让整个团队深入理解产品、客户群体以及用户面临的痛点，培养同理心，同时洞察当前的行业现状。（00:46:47） 接下来，我们会围绕这些洞察展开讨论。有时我们会调取数据分析，发现某些用户行为模式，比如某些类型的公司更频繁使用某项功能，对此我们会进行深入思考。通常，我们会带着疑问开启调研：用户为何会有这样的行为？然后对照数据分析，判断是否需要优化某项指标。最神奇的部分在于，当整个团队共同构建这种理解后，每个成员都能逐渐深化对用户和产品的认知。（00:47:40） 随后，我们会围绕具体问题展开讨论，比如“我们该如何推进下一步？”此时团队成员已充分掌握用户与产品的真实情况，因此能更清晰地制定决策，无需过度依赖数据支撑。这才是关键所在——整个团队需要持续与用户沟通，理解产品优势与不足之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I imagined you were going to say, and I love hearing that. For someone that wants to create a similar culture, is there tactically anything you find, just understand if your employees and engineers, designers have enough of that context and really understand the problem?
turns.zh: 这正是我预料到的回答，听你这么说真是太棒了。对于那些希望打造类似文化的公司而言，从战术层面看，你认为关键在于让员工（包括工程师和设计师）充分理解上下文，真正理解用户痛点吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think it's always, different people in a company will have different understandings. It's not like you can expect everyone will every day go to see everything and has this. But we do sometimes sessions with the team or we do record videos with the customers, we write notes and we share this with people. I feel like again, it's fairly apparent, if you know your customers or the product, it's a very different way you can talk about it versus if you don't have any idea. I think if you don't have any idea, you probably don't even know what to say. (00:48:59): So I think it's apparent if people have that then, it's not like every project's like we need everyone to have this understanding. Probably, usually enough if one or two people have that understanding or have different understanding of different things. So I think again, I feel like it's a culture thing. I think the other thing is you just have to kind of believe in it. (00:49:26): I think sometimes people use data a lot or too much because they're worrying or they're afraid that, will I make the wrong choice? And I'm using data to make the choice for me. But then you might still feel like this is not the right choice, but the data is telling me is the right choice and then turns out maybe it was the right choice or not. But it's more like, again, like a practice thing. I think the company and you need to be okay that sometimes we make mistakes and we made the wrong choice and then we just can fix it. But at least we made that choice and the data didn't make that choice for us.
turns.zh: 我觉得公司里的不同人总会有不同的理解。你不能指望每个人每天都去了解所有事情并掌握这些知识。不过我们有时会和团队一起开会，或者与客户录制视频，写下笔记并与他人分享。我觉得这很明显，如果你了解你的客户或产品，你谈论起它的方式就会截然不同，否则你可能根本不知道该说什么。（00:48:59）所以我认为，如果人们具备这些能力，那很明显，并不是每个项目都需要每个人都具备这种理解。通常，只要有一两个人具备这种理解，或者对不同事物有不同的理解，就足够了。所以我觉得这又是一个文化问题。我认为另一个关键点是，你必须对此有信心。（00:49:26）我觉得有时候人们过度依赖数据，可能是因为他们担心或害怕自己会做出错误的选择，然后用数据来替他们做决定。但即便如此，你可能还是会觉得这不是正确的选择，但数据却告诉你这是正确的，结果却可能并非如此。不过这更像是一种实践方法。我认为公司和个人都应该接受这样一个事实：有时我们会犯错，选择错误，但至少我们做出了选择，而不是让数据替我们做决定。

turns.en: What's interesting about-
turns.zh: 有趣的是——

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: The data didn't make that choice for us.
turns.zh: 数据没有替我们做出选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting about this is if you've heard the episode on RAMP and how Ramp builds product with Geoff Charles, there's such different ways of building product. Ramp is all about velocity, shipping all the time, metrics, measuring everything. And your approach is almost the opposite. And I think what's interesting there, as a takeaway, is just there's many ways to do it. You just have to do it almost fully and you have to have really specific people. It feels like the people want to work in a certain way. And a lot of it I think also is the founder has to be natural to the way the founder operates and thinks about building and building a company.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，如果你听过关于RAMP以及Geoff Charles如何用RAMP开发产品的节目，就会发现开发产品的方式截然不同。RAMP强调速度、持续发布、数据指标、全方位衡量。而你的方法几乎与之相反。我认为这其中有趣的一点是，尽管有许多不同的方法，但你必须全身心投入，并拥有非常专业的人才。感觉这些人希望以特定的方式工作。很多时候，我认为创始人必须要与自己的经营理念和公司发展思路相契合。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, and for sure. And then if you look at successful companies and Amazon is very different than Apple in how they operate. And I think both of them are successful, but not in the same way. (00:50:50): So I think it's, again, it's like... Yeah, it's a decision you make as a company or as a founder, what kind company you want to build. I do think there is some aspects of the domain that you're in. What does that domain and the problem space require from that company? And for us, I think it's... I think we are in the retention business. And the trust business that ideally we have a company starting use Linear very early on and then they stay with us forever. And I think the only way we can do that is we need to continuously deliver them good quality product and maintain that trust that we are... That we don't fail them more or somehow otherwise mistreat them. (00:51:36): And I think some businesses are much more transactional where it's like, yeah, we just need to make this e-commerce sale. And then once it's done, we don't care what happens. (00:51:47): So our case, it's more like we really need to build this relationship over time. And then that's why I think some of the choices we make are also more about respecting the customer versus we're just wanting to drive the revenue of the company.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。如果你观察成功的公司，就会发现亚马逊和苹果在运营方式上截然不同。我认为两者都很成功，但成功的方式却不尽相同。（00:50:50）所以我觉得，这又回到了……是的，这是一个公司或创始人必须做出的决定——你想打造怎样的公司。我认为这与你所处的领域有一定关系。你的领域和所面临的问题对公司有何要求？对我们而言，我认为我们从事的是留存业务。理想情况下，我们希望客户尽早开始使用Linear，然后与我们保持长期合作关系。而要做到这一点，我们必须持续为他们提供高质量的产品，并维护信任——不让他们失望，也不以任何方式亏待他们。（00:51:36）有些业务则更具交易性，比如只需完成一次电商交易。交易完成后，人们就不再关心后续情况了。（00:51:47）而我们的业务更像是需要逐步建立长期关系。因此，我认为我们所做的某些决策更注重尊重客户，而非单纯追求公司收入增长。

turns.en: Yeah. I don't think there's any complicated processes. turns.zh: 是的。我觉得没有什么复杂的流程。所以我觉得其中一个关键点是，我2012年参加YC时，他们强调的核心要点是——创业公司最应该专注于客户沟通、产品开发和锻炼身体。如果你发现自己在做其他事情，那很可能是在做错事。
