turns.en: And the third one you said exercise or...
turns.zh: 还有第三个你提到的，是锻炼身体还是……

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And the exercise is that it's important for you to be healthy or not just burn yourself out. So I think it was a balance [inaudible 00:54:17] to that.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。而锻炼身体对于保持健康很重要，否则你会把自己累垮的。所以我觉得这是一个平衡[00:54:17]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So I'm doing those three things. (00:54:23): I think the thinking there is, I think we often as a company also talk about this, and very early on. And I use this the same way and I think the company can use it the same way. I think there's always things that you're supposed to do or it sounds like a good idea to do. And it could be like, yeah, come to this podcast. And I actually think before it wasn't like... (00:54:47): Or I always have this question, is this important to do now or is it important to maybe do later? So I think, for example, the question on this podcast is I didn't feel like it was important to do it earlier because we weren't at the stage or a scale or something that I think it'd be as interesting or something. So I think it was a better timing to do it later. (00:55:09): Similarly, when we built the product, initially we were just very focused on is this really important thing to do? There's always like, yeah, you could get SOC 2 security certificate. And we know that eventually we need to get it, but we don't need it today. So we just say no to that. And if customer asks for it, so we say we don't have it. And we'll have it one day but not now. And see, a lot of times people are like, "Okay, that's fine." (00:55:38): And then internally, we also talk about this, you knowing RPG games, you have the main quest lines and then you have the side quest lines. And we often talk about the companies avoid the side quests. There's always ideas people have and it's a good thing and it's like people have ideas, but then it might be like, "Yeah, let's make this T-shirt, so let's make this thing." And then we're like, "Well, does it help the customers? Does it help the product?" This sounds like a side quest to me, and basically means we shouldn't do it. This doesn't progress the main quest line, which is building this product and making it awesome for these customers. (00:56:17): So it's similar to me. It's like I operate this way personally too, that I think about "Is this important for the main quest line in building this company for me? Or is this something that I can ignore for now, or something that I can do later and it makes more sense then?"
turns.zh: 所以我正在做这三件事。（00:54:23）：我认为这里的思路是，我们公司也经常谈论这个问题，而且很早之前就开始讨论了。我以同样的方式看待这个问题，我觉得公司也可以用同样的方法。我觉得总有一些事情你应该做，或者听起来是个好主意。比如，嗯，参加这个播客吧。我其实觉得之前没觉得有必要，因为我们当时还没到那个阶段或规模，我觉得那时候做这件事没那么有趣之类的。所以我觉得晚点再做会更合适。（00:55:09）：同样，当我们开发产品时，最初我们非常专注于这件事是否真的重要？总有人说，嗯，你可以获得SOC 2安全认证。我们知道最终我们需要获得它，但现在不需要。所以我们就拒绝了。如果客户要求，我们就说我们没有。以后会有的，但不是现在。很多时候人们会说，“好吧，没关系。”（00:55:38）：然后在内部，我们也讨论过这个问题，你知道RPG游戏吧，有主线任务和支线任务。我们常说公司要避免做支线任务。人们总会有一些想法，这很好，但有时就会说，“是啊，让我们做这件T恤吧，让我们做这个东西。”然后我们就会说，“嗯，这对客户有帮助吗？对产品有帮助吗？”对我来说这听起来像是支线任务，基本上意味着我们不应该做它。这不会推进主线任务，那就是为我建立这家公司。（00:56:17）：所以这对我来说也很相似。我个人也是这样运作的，我会想“这对建立这家公司的主线任务有多重要？或者这是我现在可以忽略的，或者以后做会更有意义？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such incredibly good advice. Basically ask yourself, "How important is this to do now? And is this the main quest or is this a side quest?" Amazing. (00:56:47): Okay, so let's talk about hiring. As with most areas, you're very, very, very deliberate about hiring. The bar is so insanely high at Linear, and you also hire very few people. So just a few questions along these lines, just one is when you're hiring people, what do you look for that you think maybe other people are not looking for enough? And where do you spend a lot of time?
turns.zh: 这真是非常好的建议。基本上就是问自己，“现在做这件事有多重要？这是主线任务还是支线任务？”太棒了。（00:56:47）：好的，那我们来谈谈招聘。和大多数领域一样，你们在招聘上非常、非常、非常谨慎。Linear的门槛高得离谱，而且你们招聘的人也很少。所以就几个相关问题，比如你们招聘人才时，会看重哪些方面，而其他公司可能不太重视？还有你们会花很多时间在哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think one of the things all of us founders saw in this high-growth company is that sometimes the high growth, especially on the employee side, is not that great. It can create a lot of chaos or just messiness. Or just generally in my past and working in companies, it's almost never... It was always easier to work with a smaller team, very high quality people than with a very large team of more average people. It's almost like it's always faster and better output when you have a much more smaller team. (00:57:43): That was the thing with Linear too, is we just believe that you can actually build better with less people than you can with more people. So that's the basic belief we have. So then when it goes to hiring, we've been taking very slow steps on it that in almost the first year we didn't hire anyone. Then the second year we hired a couple people, and then the second year we hired a few more. We never more than doubled in a year. And that's been our guideline that we shouldn't more than double. And this might be something we change in the future that we actually might do less than that. (00:58:20): But when we look into hiring, it is a couple things. One is also that it obviously depends on the role, but basically I would say with every role, we often talk about there needs to be some taste or some this kind of understanding of how things are done or what's the... People have more a broader perspective than whatever their role is. (00:58:46): So we talked about the engineering before that they do need to do some of this BM type of stuff. And so what we look for in them is that if they have some of this skill set or product thinking, or they can articulate why some choices are better than some others, or in their past did they disagree with some of the company's choices or the team's choices, or... So we want to have this... Obviously they need to be good developers, but also do they have this a product sensibility, or do they have a judgment around that? (00:59:22): And this goes similar to, for example, a marketing hire is... We think about, yeah, we do need the marketing skill sets, but then we also want to see that this person also maybe is a good storyteller or they have this appreciation for writing or stories or they have a taste of what's interesting and what's not. (00:59:46): So I think, or when we hire operations person, we also like to see that they maybe have understanding on HR and maybe it's not their role, but they understand it. And what happens is when you have these people that are a little bit more than their title, it's like the company is, I think, much more easier to manage because it's like people can pick up things more easily or they can work together more easily because everyone has more like a shared areas or you rarely get to the point people say it's not my job. It's more like people understand, okay, yeah, I'm kind of in operations, but today I need to help on this HR thing, which is okay. And so that's what we look for people is they are more than their... They can take more scope than their skill set would assume, or what normally is expected from them.
turns.zh: 我认为，我们所有创始人在这家高速发展的公司中发现的一个问题是，过快的增长——尤其是在员工层面——往往弊大于利。它可能会引发混乱或无序状态。以我过去在其他公司的经验来看，与规模较大但人员素质一般的团队相比，跟小而精的团队合作总是更高效、更易出成果。（00:57:43）：Linear公司的情况也是如此，我们坚信用更少的人能比用更多的人创造出更优质的产品。这是我们的核心信念。因此在招聘策略上，我们采取了极其谨慎的步骤。第一年几乎没有招聘新人；第二年只招了几个人；第三年又增加了一些。我们的招聘增长从不超过一倍。这也是我们的指导原则——招聘人数不应超过现有员工的一倍。未来我们或许会调整这一策略，考虑更低的招聘规模。（00:58:20）：招聘时我们会综合考量多个因素。首先，这取决于具体职位需求，但总的来说，我认为每个职位都需要具备一定的判断力和行业洞察力。（00:58:46）：以工程团队为例，他们确实需要掌握一些商业敏锐度。但我们更看重的是他们是否具备产品思维，能清晰解释某些决策的优劣，或是在过往工作中曾质疑公司或团队的某些决策。（00:59:22）：类似地，招聘市场人员时，我们不仅关注专业技能，更关注他们的叙事能力、文字功底以及对有趣内容的鉴赏力。（00:59:46）：对于运营人员，我们希望他们对人力资源有一定了解，即便非其专长领域也能胜任相关工作。当团队成员具备超出职位要求的能力时，公司管理会更加顺畅，因为成员能更轻松地跨部门协作，很少出现“这不是我的职责”这样的推诿。相反，他们会主动理解：“好吧，我是运营人员，但今天需要协助人力资源工作，没关系。”这正是我们所追求的员工素质——他们能超越自身技能边界，承担更多职责。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially you're looking for these Venn diagram overlappings across different functions and teammates.
turns.zh: 所以本质上，你们在寻找不同职能和团队成员之间的Venn图重叠区域。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. I think the other thing is, like I said before, is we want to build much... I think a company that has less employees, which means that it's... Like I said before, we don't want that many specialized roles or too specific areas of ownership or something. We just think that we could build this... We could have less people and those people can take on more scope and they can own more scope. (01:01:19): I think traditionally, I feel like in companies, how do you get more scope is that you advance in the levels of the company because there's a lot of different teams and different levels. And then to get any kind of scope, you need to rise into this higher levels. And what we try to do is you don't actually have to have that many levels, but people can just already, when they start, they can start owning more areas. (01:01:45): And I think that can be much more also interesting, not to everyone, but I think interesting to many people. And it's kind of like how I also always felt about us being a designer is I didn't feel like my job is purely just looking at the designs. I also thought I actually need to be helping this business or helping this other area as well. So I think it's just also natural to me.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得还有一点，就像我之前说的，我们希望打造一个…我觉得一个员工较少的公司意味着…就像我之前说的，我们不希望有太多专职岗位，或者过于细分的职责领域之类的。我们只是觉得我们可以通过…我们可以用更少的人来承担更多职责，他们可以拥有更广阔的职权范围。（01:01:19）我觉得传统上，公司里要获得更广阔的职权范围，通常需要晋升到更高的职级层级，因为公司里有各种不同的团队和职级结构。要获得这样的职权范围，你必须晋升到更高的层级。而我们尝试做的是，不需要那么多层级结构，人们一入职就能直接开始承担更广泛的职责范围。（01:01:45）我觉得这可能更有趣，虽然不是所有人都认同，但我觉得对很多人来说都很有吸引力。这也让我一直觉得，作为设计师，我的工作不只是看设计图，我还觉得自己应该为公司其他部门或业务线提供帮助。所以对我来说，这很自然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So one thing you didn't mention is you have a really unique way of interviewing, which is a paid work trial. Can you just talk about what that is? And also just while you're in that area, you talked about testing for product sensibility, so whatever you can share how you actually do that would be awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你之前没提到的是，你们有一种非常独特的面试方式，叫做带薪工作试用。你能不能讲讲这是什么意思？还有，刚刚你提到要测试产品敏感度，你能分享一下具体怎么做的吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. So we do with all of the employees, we've done a paid work trial and depends on the role, what it looks like, how long it is and depends on also sometimes on the person. But basically we do fairly standard interview loops where we test... We have some hiring manager interviews and then skill interviews or tests. And then the last step of the process is the work trial. (01:02:53): And basically, they basically come as a mini contractor to the company, and we give them a very usually fairly vague problem statements. If you're an engineer, it's like, hey, there's this feature that needs to be built. How would you build it? Then go build it. And so basically they need to first understand the problem. Then they need to scope it down to something that they can do in the timeframe that they have. And then they actually go... They get the access to a code base. They can actually go and go and build a version of it. And then at the end they can present the work they did. (01:03:29): And why we do this is that we just seeing that it's a very good way to see for both of us, both for the company and the candidates to see how we work together. And I think for the candidate, what they can see is, what kind of company are you joining, what is it like to work here, and what is [inaudible 01:03:53] ownership or how do I approach this? (01:03:55): I think a lot of engineers also like that they see the code base and they're like, oh wow, this is really clean and it's not some kind of spaghetti code type of thing situation. So I think it helps the candidates as well understand what are they signing off for, which I think can be very risky sometimes. Especially with startups, it's really hard to tell how the startup is operating just from the interviews. And in large companies, I think things are more standardized. So I think they're more similar and it's easier to make that choice. But with startups, it can be very different how companies operate.
turns.zh: 是的。我们对所有员工都这样做。我们会进行带薪工作试用，具体取决于职位要求、试用时长以及候选人自身情况。但基本上，我们会遵循比较标准的面试流程，包括面试、技能测试等环节。最后一步是工作试用。（01:02:53）：基本上，这些候选人会以临时承包商的身份加入公司，我们通常会给他们一个比较模糊的需求描述。比如，如果你是工程师，我们会说：嘿，有个功能需要开发，你会怎么实现？然后他们需要先理解问题，接着将其细化到可在既定时间内完成的范围。之后，他们可以访问代码库，开发出一个版本，最后展示成果。（01:03:29）：我们之所以这样做，是因为我们发现这对双方——公司和候选人——都是一个很好的评估合作方式。对候选人来说，他们能直观了解加入的公司是什么样的，在这里工作是什么体验，以及如何承担责任等问题。（01:03:55）：很多工程师也喜欢这样，因为他们能看到代码库，感叹‘哇，代码结构真清晰，不像某些乱七八糟的代码’。这能帮助候选人更清楚自己签约的内容，避免潜在风险。特别是初创公司，仅凭面试很难判断其运营模式，而大公司流程更规范，选择更清晰。但初创公司可能运营方式差异巨大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That is so unique and I rarely hear of a company being able to hire that way. I imagine one of the reasons you can get away with that where people don't have a full-time job for a while, while we're doing a paid trial is because Linear is such an enticing place to work. I imagine for a lot of companies they can't really do that. But I guess any thoughts on just maybe more companies can actually pull this off?
turns.zh: 是啊。这真是太独特了，我很少听说有公司能以这种方式招聘。我猜能这么做的原因之一是，候选人在试用期间不必全职工作，因为Linear确实是个极具吸引力的工作场所。我想很多公司没法这样做。但您觉得是否有更多公司可以效仿这种模式呢？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's always like if you don't ask, you don't know. I think in our case that's just been the standard and we try to work with the candidate. Let's figure out maybe we do it on the weekend or maybe we do it some other vacation holiday or something. So there can be ways we can schedule it so that it causes as little kind of problems to the candidate as possible. (01:05:16): And I think we only had only a few people probably have ever declined it. It's not like I think everyone else has been, at least after the fact, they've been happy that they did it because they felt like they had a much better sense of the company they're joining. And then also during that workshop, they can actually join our meetings, they get access to our Slack and Notion, and they also have one-on-one chats with some of the other people on the team. (01:05:43): So they already get to know people. So it's a good way for them to evaluate us as well. And then for us, it's obviously we can see... What is important for us to see is how does this person operate in this kind of environment and how do they approach problems? How do they think and are they able to make progress in a very short timeframe, which I always think it's very important for startups. In large companies, you have maybe all the time in the world to do stuff. But I think any kind of startup, even with us when we take our time doing things sometimes, it's still important. We can do things quickly if we have to.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得这句话说得没错——不问的话，你永远不会知道。就我们公司而言，这一直是我们的标准做法。我们会尽可能配合候选人，比如安排面试时间在周末，或者利用其他假期休息日等。这样既能最大限度减少对候选人的影响，又能让他们更深入了解我们公司。（01:05:16）：据我所知，只有极少数人拒绝过这项安排。大多数人事后都表示很庆幸接受了邀请，因为他们能更清楚地了解加入的公司。通过研讨会，他们还能参与我们的会议，接入Slack和Notion平台，并与团队成员进行一对一交流。（01:05:43）：这样他们就能提前认识团队成员。这也是候选人评估我们的好机会。对我们而言，关键在于观察候选人在这种环境中的表现——他们如何处理问题、思考方式如何，以及能否在短时间内取得进展。这对初创公司来说至关重要。大公司可以慢慢来，但对我们这种初创公司来说，即使有时进展缓慢，也必须高效行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. Just to close the thread on product sensibility, is there anything you could share of just how you actually help understand someone's strength and ability there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后再谈谈产品敏感度相关的问题，您能否分享一下如何评估候选人的优势和能力？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. I wouldn't say we have some kind of very scientific or some special way figure it out for this. So I think a lot of it, it's like a discussion of... And I often think ask people that... Ask about their projects and I try to go deeper. It's like why was this decision made? Why do you think the decision was made? And I might ask, "Do you think it was the right decision or did you agree on it?" Or ask about what you think you would have done differently or something. (01:07:04): So I think it's more like I'm trying to... In this area and what their answers is. And people's answers can be very different levels. Some people might be, "Yeah, I didn't like it. Which yeah, it's not opinion, but it's not based on anything. It's just like you didn't like it. You should be able to expand on it saying well, I don't like it because in this case it would not work well for this kind of users or in this kind of context or for this kind of purposes. (01:07:33): So they have more of this reasoning or some kind of rational why they think this way and they can articulate that. So I think that's what we often testing for is can they do this and how well they can do it. Then there can be very wide ranges of how people do it. And when you see someone who really thinks about this stuff, it's very clear to see that they can just talk about it forever and they can go deeper and deeper. And then some people that maybe haven't had the experience or don't think this way, they're like, yeah, I don't really know. I just built it and then seemed fine.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得我们没有什么特别科学的方法。更多的是通过深入探讨。比如，我经常会问他们关于项目的问题，深入挖掘背后的原因。比如，“为什么做出这个决策？”“你认为这个决策是否正确？”或者“如果换成你，会怎么做？”（01:07:04）：我更关注他们的答案是否有逻辑层次。有些人可能只是简单回答“不喜欢”，缺乏深层逻辑。而有的人能详细说明原因，比如“因为用户体验不佳”或者“因为缺乏上下文支持”。（01:07:33）：所以我们主要考察他们的分析能力和逻辑推理能力。这两者差距很大，有些人能深入探讨问题，而有些人则浅尝辄止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's transition to the third area I wanted to spend some time on, which is growth. And basically I'd love to just understand how Linear grows and what you figured out around growth, especially in B2B SaaS. (01:08:29): So our first question here is just how long did it take from starting to work on Linear to launching, say, V1, something that a number of people can use?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想转向我想花些时间探讨的第三个领域——增长。基本上，我们很想了解Linear是如何实现增长的，以及你们在B2B SaaS领域围绕增长做了哪些探索。（01:08:29）：那么我们的第一个问题是，从开始开发Linear到推出V1版本（即多数用户可以使用的版本），到底花了多长时间？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: So we started officially in 2019. Some, I think, months before that we were already exploring and prototyping the product. So I think we prototyped different kinds of designs a little bit. (01:08:52): And then we also, one of the things we really wanted to solve is we wanted to make the application really fast. And the way we figured out we do that is we have more of this local-based data structure where all the data lives in the client, and then it gets synced on the backends with this delta [inaudible 01:09:13]. (01:09:13): And back then, we were just exploring different off-the-shelf solutions and systems, but there was nothing really there, so we ended up building our own. And so we spent some time prototyping that. And then once we officially, I think, started working on the company in April 2019, and then we announced the company roughly mid-April, and we had this little website up with the wait list. And then I think by May we could use it ourselves. And then we started inviting some friends to try it out. (01:09:49): But then I think in June, I think we started more inviting people from the wait list. And around June, July, I think we had about, I don't know, 100, 200 users on it and maybe about 10 companies or something. And then we were in this private beta stage for almost a year. And the way we did it was just like we had this wait list of people on the wait list. There was few survey questions, like what kind of tools you use today and then why do you want to use Linear and what's the company size? (01:10:23): And we invited people based on... We invited more smaller companies using the tools we currently supported. And then also I was trying to see who is more interested versus just, I don't know, I just want to try it out type of people. And then a year later, in June, we launched it publicly. And back then maybe we already had, I don't know, several hundred of companies using it. And then we also launched the pricing and I think almost all of them... Maybe one company didn't subscribe, but everyone else subscribed to that paid plan.
turns.zh: 我们于2019年正式启动项目。在此之前的几个月，我们就已经在探索和原型设计这款产品了。（01:08:52）：当时我们特别想解决的一个问题是如何让应用程序运行得更快。我们的解决方案是采用本地化的数据结构，即所有数据都存储在客户端，然后通过后端的增量同步进行更新。（01:09:13）：当时我们探索了许多现成的解决方案和系统，但没有找到合适的，于是我们决定自主开发。这部分我们花了不少时间进行原型设计。2019年4月，我们正式开始组建公司，同年4月中旬宣布成立公司，并上线了带有等待名单的小型网站。5月，我们开始邀请朋友试用产品。（01:09:49）：6月，我们开始邀请更多等待名单上的用户。6月至7月期间，我们的用户量增长至约100-200人，可能还有10家左右的公司。之后我们进入了为期近一年的私有测试阶段。我们的筛选方式是基于等待名单中的用户，发送问卷调查，了解他们目前使用的工具、为何选择Linear以及公司规模等信息。（01:10:23）：我们优先邀请了使用我们现有支持工具的小型公司。同时，我们试图区分那些真正感兴趣的用户和只是想尝试一下的用户。一年后的6月，我们正式向公众发布产品。当时可能已有数百家公司在使用我们的服务，我们还推出了付费计划，几乎所有用户都选择了付费套餐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's a number of really interesting things here. So one is you're in private beta for a year and then a year later, you launched. How long was that period between starting to incubate and starting to build to that private beta milestone?
turns.zh: 好的，这里有几个非常有趣的点。首先，你们进行了为期一年的私有测试，然后又过了整整一年才正式上线。从开始孵化到进入私有测试阶段，这期间隔了多长时间？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's just a few months. I think just-
turns.zh: 是的，我想就几个月吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a few months of building the V1?
turns.zh: 只是几个月的时间来开发V1版本？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay. I thought it was a lot longer. That is so interesting. Okay. What a team you've got over there. (01:11:27): Okay. And then this survey piece is really interesting. I've heard a little bit about this story. So essentially you launched it on Twitter. You had kind of a following. Your founders had a bit of a following, so I think that helped build up the initial wait list. (01:11:39): But what you did there wasn't just like, hey, go sign up for a wait list and you just add email addresses. It's a survey asking them what tools they use, whether it's GitHub or something else, and then also the size of the company and their interest. And that helped you basically prioritize who to go after and who to onboard. Is that right?
turns.zh: 哇，好吧。我原以为时间会更长。太有意思了。好的。你们那边的团队真是厉害。（01:11:27）：好的。然后这个调查问卷真的很有意思。我听说过一点这个故事。基本上，就是你们在Twitter上发布了这个产品，积累了一批粉丝。你们的创始人也有一定的影响力，所以这有助于建立最初的等待名单。（01:11:39）：但你们当时做的不仅仅是让人们注册等待名单，然后收集邮箱地址。你们还做了调查，询问他们使用的工具，比如GitHub之类的，以及公司的规模和他们的兴趣。这有助于你们确定优先接触的对象和引入的用户。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. And the reason we did it, because we know that we didn't support everything and what I said before and the focus is we want to also be focused on let's just build a version that can work for some people or some companies. We don't have to try to address everyone in the world in the first months of the business. And even before, after that. So it was very selective process. And I think we were fortunate that we were able to get people sign up on a wait list and I think after a month or so we had maybe 4,000 people on the wait list. (01:12:34): And then we had this internal... I think initially it was just a very manual process, but eventually we built this invite tool that we could just send invites. But in the beginning, I would go read the actual surveys in a spreadsheet, then I copied the email, and then I emailed them the invite link from my personal email. And then I would just email them after a few days or a week and it's like, "Hey, what do you think?" (01:13:01): And the reason we... And so we would invite only like... In the beginning, we maybe invited like 10 people a week. And eventually we increased those amounts. But the reason we did it that way was that we thought that if you just invite everyone at once or a lot of people at once, all of those people are going to probably hit the same problems in this kind of software that is very early stage. So I don't know. They hit the same bug or the same problem in the software. So then they will all send us feedback like, hey, there's this problem. And then we felt like it was a wasted effort. (01:13:36): So we would just do these cohorts. Let's invite these people and then they say, hey, this is a problem. This doesn't work, or something. Then we go fix that. Then after we fix that, we invite the next cohort of people. Then they say, well, there's this thing that is needed or this doesn't work, then we fix that. (01:13:54): So for that year, we did these cohorts and then always get the feedback from the cohort saying this is wrong or this doesn't work, and then we'll fix that. So eventually, I think it was much more... I think an effective way of doing the initial development than just inviting or letting everyone to use the product right at the beginning.
turns.zh: 是的。我们之所以这么做，是因为我们知道自己不支持所有功能，正如我之前所说，我们的重点是专注于开发一个能满足部分用户或公司需求的版本。我们没必要在业务初期就试图满足全球所有用户的需求。甚至在那之后也是如此。所以整个过程非常有选择性。我觉得我们很幸运能让人们注册等待名单，大约一个月后，我们的等待名单上可能有4000人。（01:12:34）：然后我们内部……最初这是一个非常手动化的过程，但最终我们开发了一个邀请工具，可以直接发送邀请链接。但一开始，我会去阅读调查问卷中的数据，然后复制邮箱，再用个人邮箱发送邀请链接。几天或一周后，我会发邮件问他们：“嘿，你觉得怎么样？”（01:13:01）：我们之所以这么做，是因为如果一次性邀请所有人，或者一次性邀请大量用户，他们很可能都会在早期阶段遇到同样的软件问题。比如遇到同样的漏洞或问题，然后反馈给我们，这会浪费很多精力。（01:13:36）：所以我们分批次邀请这些人，然后他们会反馈问题，比如“这个功能有问题”或者“这个不行”，然后我们再修复这些问题。修复后再邀请下一批用户，再收集反馈。最终，我觉得这种分批次推进的方式比一开始就让所有人使用产品要有效得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many interesting lessons from this. I wanted to ask how you got your first 10 customers. And what I'm hearing essentially was from this wait list, you launched it on Twitter, people signed up, you picked people to let onboard, you worked with them over the course of a year to make it what they needed, and then eventually you started charging.
turns.zh: 从中学到了很多有趣的经验。我想问问你们是如何获得首批10个客户的。我听说基本上是通过等待名单，你们在Twitter上发布产品，人们注册，然后挑选用户合作，一年后开始收费。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. I think the first 10 companies using it, I think maybe a little over half. Maybe there was three friends that have startups and they used it. And then I think the majority of them were just from this wait list. But they didn't pay us anything. We didn't have pricing in the beginning or during the private beta. At some point we started building the payments function, so we just added a page in the settings that you can optionally pay.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得最初使用它的前10家公司，可能有超过一半的用户。或许有三个朋友，他们的初创公司用了这个产品。然后我认为大多数用户都是从候补名单中来的。但他们没有向我们支付任何费用。最初和私有测试阶段我们都没有定价策略。后来我们开始开发支付功能，就在设置页面中添加了一个可选付费选项。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: The page in the settings that you can optionally pay and then we just give you a slider that's, how much do you want to pay per seat? Then we just see if... I know some people paid $28 per seat and some people pay $1, but it doesn't matter, we just wanted to test the functionality and see what people think. After a year, when we launched, we already had... In the, I don't know, first week of launching, we had probably some hundreds of customers.
turns.zh: 在设置页面中，用户可以选择付费金额，然后我们会提供一个滑动条，询问他们每个席位愿意支付多少钱。结果发现，有些人支付了28美元/席位，有些人只付了1美元，但这无关紧要。我们只是想测试这个功能，看看用户反应如何。一年后，产品正式上线时，我们已经积累了……上线首周大概就吸引了几百个客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have never heard of the approach to pricing as just an actual sliding scale where people can slide the scale themselves on how much they want to pay. Did that help you figure out what to charge, or is it mostly just an experiment?
turns.zh: 我从未听说过直接让用户自己滑动滑块来设定付费金额的定价策略。这对你们定价决策有帮助吗？还是说这主要只是个实验？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I don't think it gave enough data to decide, but I think it was good to see that there was some people that went... I think that 20 was probably the maximum that people could pay, so I think there was some people that went to it and they felt like, "Actually, yeah, I really love the products. I'm happy to pay $20." I think at least it gave us some confidence that, if we charge for this and it's something under $20, there's going to be market for it.
turns.zh: 我觉得这提供的数据不足以做出决策，但至少能看出确实有用户愿意付费。我记得最高的支付金额是20美元，所以有些用户愿意支付20美元，说明他们真的很喜欢我们的产品。我们从中获得了信心——如果定价低于20美元，市场应该会接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear about the story of how you've started to feel product market fit, whatever that means to you. When did you start to feel like, "Wow, this is actually going to work and maybe this is going to be a real business"?
turns.zh: 我想听听你们是如何开始感受到产品与市场的适配性的，无论你们对这个概念如何理解。什么时候你们开始觉得，“哇，这个产品真的能成功，或许这真能成为一项真正的业务”？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I think we've always been, I don't know, some paranoid or... I guess maybe a paranoid is a good way about the product market fit. I think it's paranoid in a way, we are always wondering, "Do we really have it?" And, "With who do we have it?" I think it's true in our business, that... I think we started feeling it very early on, and when people first started using it and we could see, "Now the whole company is using it and they seem happier using it and the feedback is good and they might have some additional asks for us," but we started feeling like there was definitely a product market fit with certain customer and these were more smaller, early-stage companies maybe where the founder is still running the product and they care about the speed of the shipping or they have certain values in a way, so it was a good fit with them. (01:17:27): Then I think we always know that we want to address the whole market and also just these early-stage customers, but we knew that if a Fortune 500 company came to us then, or even today, we might not be... I don't think we can provide them the solution today that works for them, so I don't think the fit is there. For us, the way we think about is, "Do we have the fit in the specific segments?" And how strong that fit is. In the company's journey, the first year, we just focused on, "Can we get the fit..." In the first two years, we focused on, "Can we get the fit in the early stage startup segment?" Basically, the goal was, "We want to be the default for startups, the default tool that the startups pick, and I think we were able to accomplish that, but we just purely focused on that segment and getting the product market fit there. (01:18:28): At the same time, we started getting some larger companies and we saw, "Yeah, it's not really great for you right now, but let's work on it, making it better," so I think the last two years we've been focusing on that. It's like, "How do we make the software work better? How do we get the product market fit stronger in this larger company segments that are hundreds of people or 1000 people?"
turns.zh:
是的，我觉得我们一直都有些多疑，或者……我猜或许多疑是判断产品市场匹配度的一个好方法。从某种程度上说，我们确实存在这种多疑心理，总在疑惑：“我们真的具备产品市场匹配吗？”以及“我们与谁达成了这种匹配？”在我们业务中确实如此……我们很早就开始感受到这一点，当人们刚开始使用我们的产品时，我们能看到“现在整个公司都在用它，他们使用起来似乎更开心了，反馈也很不错，可能还会有额外的需求”，但我们逐渐意识到，与某些客户群体确实存在产品市场匹配，尤其是那些规模较小的初创公司，比如创始人仍亲自负责产品开发的公司，他们更关注交付速度或秉持特定的价值观，所以与他们匹配度很高。

（01:17:27）然后，我们一直知道自己既想覆盖整个市场，也想服务这些初创客户，但我们知道，如果一家《财富》500强企业在当时或现在找上门来，我们可能无法为他们提供有效的解决方案，所以产品市场匹配度并不存在。对于我们来说，关键在于“在特定细分领域是否具备匹配度”，以及这种匹配度有多强。在公司发展初期，我们专注于“能否实现匹配”；前两年，我们专注于“能否在初创公司细分领域实现匹配”。我们的目标是成为初创公司的默认选择，成为他们首选的工具，我认为我们成功做到了。但我们纯粹专注于这个细分领域，努力在那里实现产品市场匹配。

（01:18:28）与此同时，我们开始接触一些大公司，发现“目前这款产品对你们来说不太实用，但让我们一起改进吧”，所以过去两年我们一直致力于此。我们在思考：“如何让软件更好地运作？如何在拥有数百或数千名员工的大型公司中强化产品市场匹配？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is such a good way and smart way of thinking about product market fit. A lot of people see product market fit as this binary, "I have it or I don't," and, "When am I going to really feel product market fit?" What you're describing is what I often hear, it's more of this spectrum of more and more confidence that there's product market fit and, even more specifically, it's product market fit with segments of the market. It's this map of the world and you're just slowly acquiring territory in the market with specific elements and then, over time, it grows and grows.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一种思考产品市场匹配的明智方法。很多人将产品市场匹配视为二元对立：“要么有，要么没有”，以及“何时才能真正感受到产品市场匹配？”你所描述的正是我们常听到的情况，更像是一个谱系，随着对产品市场匹配度的信心逐渐增强，甚至更具体地说，是与特定市场细分领域的匹配。这就像一张世界地图，你在市场中逐步占领领土，随着时间推移，影响力不断扩大。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I think a spectrum is a good way to think about it, too. I feel like there's this blog post written in the past where you know when you have product market fit and I think it probably... It's like that for some, I don't know, social consumer apps. If it's taking off or not, then you don't really have a lot of different segments, or you don't really think about it, you have millions of users and then you see it's taking off, so you have a product market fit. I think in more like a B2B world. I think there's always... You can have different sizes of customers, you can have different domains the customers are in, or there's different categories where you might be doing really well in one category and then not that well another. (01:20:14): I think maybe the countering to do things is that, actually, if you're doing really well in some category, just double down on that. This is something I talked to the Zoom founder, Eric, at some point in the company's lifecycle, and this is also what he said. When they were building Zoom in the early days, they would get this one type of customer. I don't know, maybe it's a university and then it worked really well for them. Then they're like, "How do we get more of the universities?" They would always focus on a certain customer rather than, "Let's just try to get everyone, so let's focus on everything," which is not possible. Again, it's about the focus. If you see that something is working really well, then it's almost like you should focus on doing that more until you hit some point. It's like, "Okay, now we do have that category captured or handled as much as we want," and we should expand to new area.
turns.zh: 是的，我也觉得用光谱来思考这个问题很不错。我觉得之前有篇博客文章讲过如何判断产品与市场的契合度，我觉得可能……对于某些社交消费类应用来说就是这样。如果产品火了或者没火，那你其实不会有太多不同的细分市场，或者说你不会去刻意考虑这些问题。当你有数百万用户时，如果产品火了，那就说明产品与市场契合了。但在B2B领域就不同了。你可能有不同规模的客户，客户所在的不同领域，或者在某个类别中表现出色而在另一个类别中表现不佳。（01:20:14）我觉得应对这种情况的策略是，如果某个类别表现出色，那就继续深耕。这是我在Zoom创始人Eric的职业生涯某个阶段与他交流过的，他也这么说的。早期开发Zoom时，他们先获得了一类客户，比如某所大学，然后效果很好。接着他们会想：“如何获取更多这类客户呢？”他们总是专注于某个特定客户群体，而不是试图面面俱到，这根本不可能。关键在于聚焦。如果某件事效果很好，那就应该持续深耕，直到达到目标。比如：“好，我们已经在这个类别中占据了足够的份额，现在该拓展新领域了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Essentially, look for pull and just follow that and pay attention to that.
turns.zh: 本质上，要寻找市场的需求并顺势而为。

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. I think, for us, there can be sometimes... For example, now we have... Most of the AI companies are using us, so I think it's always... Before that, it was a crypto company, so I think there's... When we see these kinds of things happening, then we start to think like, "Could we do something differently or could we get more of these AI companies on board?"
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得对我们来说，偶尔也会有……比如现在我们有……大多数AI公司都在用我们的服务，所以我觉得这始终……在此之前，是一家加密货币公司，所以我觉得……当我们看到这些情况发生时，就会思考：“我们能否做出不同的尝试，或者能否让更多AI公司加入我们？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a great lesson. Just a few more questions, you mentioned that you launched on Twitter and that led to a large wait list and a growing wait list. Is there anything you did before that to build this following? That sounds really amazing, "Cool, we just announced it on Twitter and we have this large wait list and then we grow and we get all these customers." Is there anything you did ahead of time in anticipation of this launch? Would you recommend people work on building some kind of following online before they work in a startup? Was it just like, "Hey, we happen to have this following," and it worked out? Anything along those lines you would recommend to founders these days?
turns.zh: 真是个深刻的教训。再问几个问题，你提到在Twitter上发布消息后，获得了长长的等待名单。发布前有没有做过什么积累粉丝的工作？这听起来太神奇了，“哇，我们刚在Twitter上宣布，就有这么长的等待名单，然后用户不断涌入。”发布前有没有做过准备工作？你会建议创业者在创业前先积累一些线上粉丝吗？还是说就是碰巧有了这些粉丝，然后就成功了？对于如今的创业者，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. I think definitely if you have a following and, obviously, depends on what kind of following, but I think my background as a designer, I would say at Airbnb and Coinbase and other places, and I did some talks in conferences and write some blog posts. I was definitely out there and had some of that following, which was helpful, but it wasn't like I have hundreds of thousands of followers or millions, or something. I had maybe 10,000 or something, which is a significant number, but then I think the other thing is... I think with the announcement, one of the things we did, I think, well is I think sometimes startups do try to emulate successful, large companies too much and you do this fancy announcements where it's like, "Hey, now we are doing this fancy thing and it sounds very corporate or something." (01:23:17): With our announcement, we wrote it more direct or authentic to us like, "This is what we're going to do and this is why, and these are some of the things we're going to do." On a Twitter, we did the same thing. All of us founders, we wrote our own reasons why we're doing this, and I think it was just much more... I think people like us could resonate more with it, so we were writing to the right audience. I think that's probably the first thing when you're announcing your company, you think about, "Who is my first audience? Who would be the best early users for this product and where are they?" And then, "How do they think about things and what kind of language do they use?" For us, it came very naturally, because we are these people. (01:24:09): We are in building software and these companies, and other people have seen similar things we have seen, so I think the way we announced it resonated with a lot of people. Then I think we did have some friends... I said we got some angel round where we got some friends involved. The main reason we did it was that we just felt like, in the early days, it's good to have... You feel like a real company in a way, that you have someone to answer for in a way. Even though the investors normally run your company or they don't have that much power, it's more like, "I took someone's money so I now need to make it worth it," kind of. With the announcement, again, we could use some of those people to spread the message as well.
turns.zh:
是的。我认为，如果你有一定的影响力——当然，这取决于你所拥有的粉丝群体规模——但以我作为设计师的背景为例，我曾在Airbnb和Coinbase等公司工作，参加过一些会议演讲，也写过博客文章。我确实在业内积累了一批粉丝，这对我的事业有所助益，但我并没有数十万或数百万的粉丝——我大概有1万名粉丝，这已经是一个不小的数字了。另外，我觉得在公司发布声明时，我们采取了更直接、更真实的沟通方式。比如，我们在Twitter上发布声明时，所有创始人都亲自撰写了开发信函，解释我们的初衷和产品定位。这种真诚的表达更能引起目标受众的共鸣，符合我们的品牌定位。

在宣布公司成立初期，你首先要考虑的问题应该是：“谁是我们的核心受众？谁会成为我们产品的首批用户？他们身处何处？”然后，“他们如何看待产品，又使用怎样的语言？”对我们来说，这一切都顺理成章，因为我们本身就是软件开发者，我们的经历与其他初创公司十分相似。这种亲身实践的经验让我们的宣讲更能引发共鸣。

在融资angel round时，我们确实邀请了部分朋友参与投资。主要原因是我们认为，在初创阶段，有外部投资者的参与能提升公司的专业感，让我们更有责任感，即便投资方通常不直接管理公司，但这会形成一种隐含的约束力——“既然拿了别人的钱，就必须证明其价值”。通过宣讲活动，我们也成功动员了这些朋友为我们传播信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close out our conversation, just a couple more broad questions. You have a pretty unique culture at Linear, and I know one fun thing that you do is you have this baking competition. Can you talk about that and what it is you do there?
turns.zh: 在结束对话之前，我想再问几个宏观问题。Linear的企业文化非常独特，我知道你们有一项很有趣的活动——烘焙比赛。能跟我们讲讲这项活动吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah. Since we are a fully remote and distributed company, so we have people in Europe and US, a lot of group gatherings are challenging. Remote group sessions are challenging, because the time zones are so different, so some of the basic things, like happy hours, don't really work that well. Also, Zoom happy hours is probably not that fun anyway. I think a lot of people in the company watch The Great British Baking Show, so we decided, "Maybe we do something like that," where basically, we would just pick a recipe. Firstly, it was baking, now we expanded to cooking recipes, too. We just pick a recipe that is somewhat reasonable to do in a few hours, in a couple of hours, and it doesn't require tons of equipment or skill, or something. Then we just tell people, "Go buy the ingredients, use the company card," everyone has a company card, "And then hop on Zoom on this day." (01:26:18): For me, since I'm in California, it's like 8:00 AM, so we started the baking or cooking then. We've made things like roll cake and lemon meringue pie, and we made some [Portuguese 01:26:35], which is Portuguese pastry. Then we just hop on the Zoom, everyone's doing their thing, following the recipe, and then sometimes people have questions like, "Hey," I don't know, "I'm stuck with this," or, "My dough looks weird, does your dough look like this?" People can help each other and then also chitchat about whatever random things at the same time. Then we do the thing and then everyone takes pictures and posts on the Slack channel, it's what they achieved. I think we have friendly competitions like who did it best, so people sometimes put a lot of effort into the decorations and visuals. (01:27:17): In a way, it's, again, a craft thing that we do. I think baking and cooking and these kinds of things are also a craft, so we liked it that way. Yeah, we've been basically doing it quarterly since the beginning of the company. Yeah, the latest thing, we were a little bit... I think didn't have that much time, because we decided to do an easier thing, which is a summer drink recipe, so I think people made matcha drinks and some coconut drinks or white iced tea, or something. Yeah, that was interesting to do.
turns.zh: 是啊。因为我们是一家完全远程分布式公司，所以我们在欧洲和美国的员工很多，组织集体聚会确实挺有挑战的。远程团队会议也很难办，因为时区差异太大，像欢乐时光这类基本活动效果不佳。再说了，Zoom上的欢乐时光可能也挺无聊的。公司里很多人都喜欢看《英国烘焙大赛》，所以我们就想，"不如搞点类似的活动"。基本上，我们会选一个食谱。最初是烘焙，现在也扩展到烹饪食谱了。我们会挑一个几个小时内能完成的食谱，不需要太多设备或高超技巧的那种。然后告诉大家，"去买食材，用公司卡支付"（每人都有公司卡），再约定某个时间上Zoom平台。（01:26:18）对我来说，因为我在加州，时间是早上8点，所以我们那时候就开始烘焙或烹饪了。我们做过卷蛋糕、柠檬蛋白派，还有葡萄牙糕点之类的。然后大家各自操作，按照食谱步骤来，偶尔有人会问问题，比如"哎呀，这个卡住了"，或者"我的面团看起来好奇怪，你的面团是这样吗？"大家互相帮助，同时也会闲聊各种随机话题。最后大家拍照发到Slack频道里，展示成果。我们还会评选最佳作品，有时候大家会很用心装饰和摆盘。（01:27:17）总之，这就是我们喜欢做手工活动的原因。烘焙、烹饪这类事儿本身也是一门手艺，所以我们很享受这个过程。从公司成立开始，我们基本每个季度都会举办这样的活动。最近一次，我们有点……时间不够，所以就简化成了夏日饮品食谱，大家做了抹茶饮品、椰子汁、白冰茶之类的，挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you ever won one of these competitions yourself?
turns.zh: 你自己有没有参加过这些比赛并获奖？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I don't know if we declare winners that much, but I do think I do... Since I'm a designer, I do have some advantages on the visual presentation, so I think that I generally do well on that. Obviously, with this remote competition, that's the only thing you can really look for. It's not necessarily about the taste or the texture, because you can't really taste it through the Zoom.
turns.zh: 我不知道我们是否经常评选获奖者，但我确实……作为设计师，我在视觉呈现方面有优势，所以在这方面通常表现不错。当然，远程比赛的话，就只能看这个环节了。毕竟口味和口感没法通过Zoom传达。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe as a last question, just again broadly, you've gone from being an IC designer, manager of designers, to the CEO of very fast-growing company. What's something that you've learned about leadership over the journey of Linear that maybe you didn't expect?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，宏观一点说，你从IC设计师、设计师管理者，成长到快速发展的公司的CEO，这一路走来，对领导力有什么深刻体会，是否有出乎意料的收获？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: For some reason, it was surprising to me, I think, that being a CEO or some of these leadership roles is that you end up doing so many different things. When I was a designer, even if I would be some high-level designer in some company, you're just mostly focusing on the design and that's your job, but then when you're a CEO, then every week or every day, there's some different thing going on. Sometimes there can be problems, but a lot of times, it's like, "Hey, we need to figure out how we're going to do this. How are we going to do this compensation?" Or, "How are we going to do this marketing plan?" Or, "How are we going to do this offsite thing?" What's definitely challenging for me is handling that different kinds of things that come to you and staying somewhat focused, still, on something. (01:29:42): I think I haven't necessarily fully figured it out, but I also figured it out, that hiring and delegation helps with this, that if you can find other leaders that can take on certain areas, that's helpful. That's the main thing, that it's a very wide range of things that you maybe didn't have experience before, but also, I think it's interesting for me to learn about these things. You learn about the financials and you learn about legal things, and then you start to feel like, "Actually, I know something about this thing," over time.
turns.zh: 出于某种原因，我觉得担任CEO或其他领导职务后，要处理的事情实在太多样化，这让我感到惊讶。当我还是设计师时，即使在某家公司担任高级设计师，工作也主要专注于设计本身。但成为CEO后，每周甚至每天都会有各种不同的事情要处理。有时会遇到问题，但更多时候是诸如“我们需要如何处理这个薪酬方案？”、“如何制定营销计划？”或者“如何组织一次团建活动？”之类的事务。对我来说，最具挑战性的是要处理各种突如其来的事务，同时还要保持对核心工作的专注。（01:29:42）我觉得自己还没有完全搞清楚，但也总结出了一些经验：招聘和授权能有效缓解这种压力，若能找到能胜任不同领域的领导者，无疑是件好事。这才是关键所在——你会遇到许多以前从未接触过的领域，但探索这些领域的过程本身也很有趣。比如，你会了解财务知识、法律条款，久而久之，你会发现自己对某些领域已然驾轻就熟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For the actual final question, before we get to very exciting lightning round, what's just the future of Linear? What's coming? What's happening in the future? Anything you can share?
turns.zh: 接下来是最后一个问题，正式进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。Linear的未来前景如何？接下来会有哪些新动态？能否分享一些信息？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's always things we're working on and improving. One, a newer thing we're working on is this feature called Asks. Basically, what it is is that... We see that, in a company, there can be a lot of different people that need to interact with the product team or different people that need to interact with this team, but they're not necessarily in Linear or part of this team. We'd be building this an Ask feature, which is an integration to Slack where you can very easily go to a Slack channel and then ask your question. You need something from this team, maybe it's the IT team, that you need a laptop, or maybe it's the infrastructure team and you need something from them, then the team that is handling the request, they can very easily send it to Linear, into this triage that we have, and then they can start doing stuff with it. (01:31:26): If they have questions or additional questions to the actual person who requested it, we can send those messages back to the person through Slack, so they don't actually have to go to Linear or they don't have to be a Linear user to use it. We think this is just a good way for the company, or the whole company, to be more potentially involved in the product operations without having to be a power user of Linear, because not every function really uses it or needs to use it.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为我们始终在持续改进和创新。目前正在开发的新功能叫做“Asks”。其核心理念是……我们发现，在公司里，许多需要与产品团队或其他团队互动的人，并非身处Linear平台或属于该团队。比如，IT部门需要为某人配发笔记本电脑，或者基础设施团队需要提供某项支持时，团队成员可以通过Slack直接向对应频道提出请求。被请求的团队可以将任务同步到Linear平台的分流系统中，然后展开后续处理。（01:31:26）若有后续疑问或补充问题，用户可通过Slack将消息发送回原请求者，完全无需登录Linear平台或成为其用户。我们认为，这为整个公司提供了更便捷的参与产品运营的方式，无需成为Linear的高级用户，因为并非每个部门都需要深度使用该平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What a cool peek at something coming out soon, or maybe out by the time this comes out. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got a bunch of questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。能提前一睹这款即将上线（或在本期播客发布时即将发布）的功能，真是令人兴奋。接下来进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。我准备了一堆问题，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I'm ready.
turns.zh: 是的，我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的。你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Timeless Way of Building by Christopher Alexander. He wasn't really an architect, but he, I think, taught in Berkeley. He has these interesting thoughts about building things and he focuses on buildings and towns and these kinds of spaces, but I think there's a lot of things that are also interesting for building software. The other book that I like is the Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, because it also talks about the quality of things and I think that's one of the main themes of the book. The thing is also that quality is so hard to define. If you actually start thinking about it, it's like, how do you define it? It's really hard to pin down, but it's like when you try something or see it, then you know if it's quality or not.
turns.zh: 克里斯托弗·亚历山大（Christopher Alexander）的《永恒的建造之道》。他其实不是建筑师，但我记得他曾在伯克利任教。他对建筑、城镇及各类空间有着许多有趣的见解，但我认为其中很多观点对软件开发也很有启发。另一本我很喜欢的书是《禅与摩托车维修艺术》，因为它也探讨了事物的品质问题，我认为这是该书的主旨之一。然而，品质的定义实在太难了。当你深入思考时，会发现如何定义它？这实在难以捉摸，但当你亲身尝试或观察某物时，就能判断它是否具有品质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some recent movies or TV shows you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近看过哪些很喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think that the movie is probably John Wick 4. Obviously, there's no story in that movie, but I think it's very true to its nature, so I like that fact. Also, recently, I started watching the Silo on Apple TV, and I think I like it. It's like a good mystery and then, also, it reminds me of the Fallout games, so I like it that way, too.
turns.zh: 我觉得可能是《疾速追杀4》。显然这部电影没有什么故事性，但我觉得它忠实于自身特质，所以我喜欢这一点。最近我开始在Apple TV上看《地堡》，我觉得不错。这是一部不错的悬疑剧，而且让我想起了《辐射》系列游戏，所以我也很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually read the Silo books and I was really excited for the show to come out, but I mentioned this on a previous podcast, the show is so little to do with actual books. The core ideas are the same, but there's all these stories that they're just making up on the show, so I stopped watching, because that's not what I was hoping for, but-
turns.zh: 实际上我读过《地堡》系列书籍，当这部剧上线时我很兴奋，但我在之前的播客里提到过，剧集和原著几乎毫无关联。核心理念是相似的，但剧中很多故事都是虚构的，因此我没继续看下去，因为这和我期待的不一样，不过——

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Okay, interesting. Maybe I need to check the books later, once I watch the show.
turns.zh: 好的，有意思。或许我之后需要看看原著书籍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Definitely, read the books, but there's three of them and only the first one is actually good. The other ones are not actually very good and I should not have read them, because it just went off the rails a little bit. Anyway, next question. What is a favorite interview question that you'd like to ask candidates when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 是的，一定要读原著书籍，但共有三本，只有第一本还不错。其他两本质量不高，我本不该读的，因为情节有些偏离轨道。不管怎样，下一个问题。当你面试候选人时，最喜欢问他们什么样的面试问题？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think, usually, I like to ask, what is the candidate most proud of and why? On their professional life or otherwise, what they're most proud of and why. Then I think we can go deeper on that, but I think it gives you a little bit of indication, what the person values and how they think about things. Also, I think it's always nice that people can share something they think they did really well and we can spend time on it versus just asking something more like negative things.
turns.zh: 我通常喜欢问，候选人最引以为傲的是什么，以及原因？无论是在职业生涯中还是其他方面，他们最引以为傲的事情以及原因。然后我们可以深入探讨，但我认为这能让你略微了解这个人的价值观和思考方式。另外，我觉得让人们分享自己做得很好的事情总是很不错的，我们可以花时间探讨，而不只是问一些负面的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some favorite products you've recently discovered that you really, really like?
turns.zh: 最近你发现了哪些非常喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I'm not sure if I discovered them recently, but recently in this home office, I've been installing some of these hue lights and I really like them, because throughout the day, I can have more harsh lighting, because I'm in meetings or something, and then in the evening, I can change the temperature. I make it much more red or orange, or something. I think it's nice that you can transition the space. It's like, "Okay, now I'm working and now I'm doing something else." You can use the lights to indicate that.
turns.zh: 我不确定是否最近发现的，但最近在家庭办公室里，我安装了一些Hue灯，我很喜欢它们。因为白天我需要更强烈的光线，比如开会之类的，晚上我可以调整色温。我把它调成更偏红或橙的颜色。我觉得能让空间过渡很棒。比如，“好的，我现在要工作了，现在要做别的事了。”你可以用灯光来暗示这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool. Do you automate the schedule or you manually change the color?
turns.zh: 太酷了。你是自动调整日程还是手动更改颜色？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Yeah, I just manually change it. On my home app, I have scenes that... There's the night scene and then there's the day scene, or the morning scene, so I just click that button and then it changes the lights.
turns.zh: 是啊，我就是手动改的。在我的家居应用里，我设了场景……有夜间场景和白天场景，或者早晨场景，只要点击那个按钮，灯光就会切换。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is extremely cool, I'm going to try that myself. What is a favorite life motto that you like to repeat yourself or share with people? Something you come back to a lot.
turns.zh: 这太酷了，我也要试试看。你有没有什么最喜欢的座右铭，喜欢反复说给别人听，或者经常回想的？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: Go slow to go fast. I think, for me, it's about that. Sometimes people have a tendency to rushing into things and especially, I think, in startups, but other places too, you have this like... I think urgency is important, but then sometimes you have too much urgency and you are rushing things, and what happens is that you rushed it and now you need to come back to fix it. I think sometimes I like to think that you should take some time to actually think about it and, "What are you going to do?" And then do it. In the end, it's going to be faster that way than going back and forth and fixing things.
turns.zh: 欲速则不达。我觉得对我来说就是这个道理。有时候人们容易急于求成，尤其是创业公司，但其他地方也一样，你会有这种……我觉得紧迫感很重要，但有时候太过急于求成，就会把事情搞砸。最后反而需要回头去修正。我觉得有时候我会想，你应该花点时间好好想想，“接下来要做什么？”然后再行动。这样比来回折腾、修修补补要快得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the most valuable lesson that your mom or your dad taught you?
turns.zh: 你妈妈或爸爸教给你的最宝贵的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: I think it's respecting people and things. I think the people respect is pretty obvious, but I think with the things you have, also, I think you should take good care of them when you use them. I don't know, clean them or put them away, and then they're ready for the next time. I think I like that, though. Rather than you treating things like they're trash or not that valuable, you should treat things that they are valuable.
turns.zh: 我觉得就是尊重人和物。我觉得尊重人这点挺明显的，但对于物品也要好好爱护。不知道，清理干净或者收好，就能为下次使用做好准备。我挺喜欢这样的。而不是把东西当成垃圾或者不值钱的东西，要知道它们是有价值的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You were born in Finland, I think you grew up in Finland. What is a Finnish food that people should definitely try to get as soon as they can?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你出生在芬兰，我想你在芬兰长大的。有什么芬兰美食是人们一定要尽快尝试的？

turns.speaker: Karri Saarinen
turns.en: One is this salmon soup, and it might sound weird, a fish soup, maybe it's not going to be that interesting. It's a creamy soup, it's on potatoes, carrots, and other things, and it's almost like a little bit of sweet flavor to it. You can make it yourself at home or you can... If you go to Finland, there's probably always a few restaurants that offer it.
turns.zh: 一种三文鱼汤，可能听起来有点奇怪，鱼汤，可能没那么有趣。这是一道奶油汤，里面有土豆、胡萝卜之类的，还有点甜味。你可以在家自己做，或者去芬兰的话，很多餐厅都有这道菜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, amazing. Is that something we could get here or you have to go to Finland to get it?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我们这儿能买到吗？还是得去芬兰才能吃到？
